questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with moderate medial knee OA asks what single change would most reduce his risk of the disease progressing and of OA developing in the other knee. Which is the most important modifiable risk factor for knee OA?
questions.explain: Body mass sets the magnitude of joint load, and weight loss of ~5 kg is associated with ~50% lower knee-OA risk. Age is not modifiable. Weight is the answer the WFQ key gives; weakness and metabolic factors also contribute.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old soccer player had an ACL reconstruction 2 years ago and now has a stable knee. She asks whether the surgery removed her risk of arthritis. What is the best response?
options: Yes, reconstruction restores normal joint loading
No: about half develop knee OA 10–20 years after ACL tear, and repair hasn't been shown to prevent it
Only meniscal tears cause post-traumatic OA
Her risk is lower than the general population's
questions.explain: Around 50% have knee OA 10–20 years after an ACL tear, and there is no evidence that surgical repair prevents OA: biomechanics are permanently altered (Mr. H's right knee). Meniscal tears/meniscectomy raise risk 4–6×.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old has severe knee pain, poor sleep and low mood, yet her X-ray shows only mild joint-space narrowing. Her neighbour has grade 4 changes and little pain. Which statement best explains this mismatch?
options: The radiologist has under-read her film
OA pain reflects intra- and extra-articular factors, including synovitis, weakness, sleep, depression and central sensitization, that X-ray can't show
She must have an inflammatory arthritis
An MRI would fully explain her pain
questions.explain: Structure and symptoms correlate poorly. Pain comes from joint factors (synovitis, effusion, cartilage defects, weakness) and extra-articular ones (genetics, sleep, depression, catastrophizing, central sensitization). X-ray shows only bone; MRI shows nothing about biopsychosocial factors.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old with severe bilateral hip OA has been almost completely sedentary for years and now has type 2 diabetes and a recent MI. Through what main mechanism is OA thought to raise cardiovascular disease and mortality?
options: Direct cardiotoxicity of cartilage breakdown products
Walking limitation leading to sedentary behaviour
Chronic NSAID use in every patient
questions.explain: OA's excess CVD, diabetes and mortality is largely driven by walking disability and sedentary behaviour. 60–90% of OA patients have another chronic condition; OA is 'not just a bit of arthritis'.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman presents with knee pain. Which feature would make you LESS likely to diagnose osteoarthritis?
questions.explain: OA is chronic and insidious; acute onset should prompt thoughts of crystals, infection, a meniscal tear or fracture. An effusion may or may not be present, crepitus is common, and a normal X-ray doesn't exclude symptomatic OA (WFQ).

questions.stem: A healthy 42-year-old accountant has 4 weeks of localized medial knee pain and swelling after twisting while playing tennis. X-ray is normal; MRI shows a medial meniscus tear. He has had no treatment. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explain: Non-surgical management first: >50% of meniscal tears settle by 8–12 weeks, although tears rarely heal, so physio builds strength and improves prognosis. Surgery only after failed conservative care or major QoL impact (WFQ).

questions.stem: A 72-year-old has medial knee pain with a normal knee exam. He also reports groin pain, and passive internal rotation of the hip is limited and reproduces his pain. What is the most likely source?
questions.explain: The hip and lower lumbar spine are the commonest sources of referred knee pain. Hip clues: groin pain and limited, irritable internal rotation. Always examine the joint above.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old with knee OA and a recurrent effusion develops sudden posterior knee and calf pain with calf swelling after gardening. What must be done first?
questions.explain: A ruptured Baker's cyst (a posterior herniation of synovium due to an effusion) mimics DVT, so DVT must be excluded. Then treat symptoms and the cause of the effusion. Never aspirate from behind the knee (neurovascular bundle).

questions.stem: On examining a 70-year-old's knee you sweep fluid up the medial side, then stroke the lateral side and see a wave refill the medial fossa. Ballottement is negative. What does this indicate?
questions.explain: A positive bulge sign = small effusion. Large effusions can't be swept (bulge negative) and are detected by ballottement or patellar tap. The sign extinguishes with repetition, so the first sweep counts.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old distance runner has lateral knee pain during runs, maximal at about 30° of flexion, with a snapping sensation and tenderness over the lateral femoral condyle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explain: ITB syndrome: friction of the iliotibial band over the lateral femoral condyle with repetitive flexion/extension, peaking near 30°. PFPS is anterior; pes anserinus is medial, ~5 cm below the joint line.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old with knee OA wants the single therapy with the greatest effect on symptoms and the lowest risk of adverse effects. Which do you recommend?
questions.explain: Exercise therapy is the most effective non-surgical treatment for hip/knee OA with no serious adverse events, and works regardless of X-ray severity. Weight loss matters but has a smaller effect alone; NSAIDs and acetaminophen carry more risk (WFQ).

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman with knee and hip OA asks whether she should take glucosamine and chondroitin from the health food store. What is the best counselling?
options: They are moderately effective for pain and function
They work only as intra-articular injections
Trials show they accelerate cartilage loss
Generally not recommended: benefit hasn't been clinically proven, though harm is unlikely
questions.explain: Not recommended: no proven clinical benefit (some placebo effect), but no contraindication and unlikely harm (WFQ). The lecture lists glucosamine as uncertain and chondroitin as not recommended.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old says 'Tylenol doesn't work' for his knee OA. He takes one 500 mg tablet occasionally. What is the best next step with his analgesia?
options: Declare acetaminophen a failure and start oral naproxen
Prescribe 1000 mg per dose on a regular schedule for a 2-week trial, checking for duplicate products
Stop analgesics and refer for arthroplasty
questions.explain: 500 mg PRN is not a therapeutic trial. Give 1000 mg per dose, scheduled (e.g. BID), for 2 weeks within daily limits (the tutor used a 3 g/day ceiling), and check for other acetaminophen products. Done properly this can delay surgery for years. Opioids and oral NSAIDs are poor choices in older adults.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with knee OA, T2DM with nephropathy and hypertension on ramipril, and a sulfa allergy needs better analgesia after a proper acetaminophen trial. Which option is most appropriate?
questions.explain: Topical NSAIDs have ~5–10% of oral systemic exposure and are first-line with comorbidity. Oral NSAIDs threaten his kidneys (nephropathy + ACEi) and BP; celecoxib contains a sulfonamide, so it's out with a sulfa allergy; opioids commit him to long-term use.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with knee OA takes apixaban and bisoprolol for atrial fibrillation. His pain flares and his daughter suggests ibuprofen. What is the best advice?
options: Ibuprofen is fine if taken with food
Avoid oral NSAIDs: combined with an anticoagulant they sharply raise bleeding risk
Use naproxen instead, since it has the lowest CV risk
Stop apixaban for the week of ibuprofen
questions.explain: Anticoagulant + NSAID is a hard stop (the CBL quoted ~10–20× bleeding risk). Use topical NSAIDs, scheduled acetaminophen or an IA steroid instead. Stopping anticoagulation risks stroke.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with diabetic knee OA receives an intra-articular corticosteroid injection. Which counselling point is most important?
options: Monitor blood glucose closely for several days afterward
questions.explain: IA steroids give weeks of relief and are 'a really good intervention', but they can cause transient hyperglycemia in diabetics, so check sugars. A steroid injection that fails is usually not repeated before considering surgery.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with knee OA stopped walking because it hurt during and after. How much pain during exercise is acceptable to tell him?
options: None: any pain means joint damage
Mild pain is allowed if it settles within about 24 hours; hurt is not harm
Any level, as long as he takes an opioid first
He should exercise only on pain-free days
questions.explain: Pain during exercise is allowed: the lecture accepts a rise of no more than 2–3/10 (GLA:D up to ~5/10) that settles within 24 h. Walking does not damage the knee and likely protects it (cartilage needs cyclical loading).

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with classic bilateral knee OA on history and exam asks what tests confirm the diagnosis. You plan to start drug therapy. Which is the most appropriate investigation plan?
options: ESR, CRP, RF and ANA to exclude inflammatory arthritis
No diagnostic tests; CBC, creatinine/eGFR and LFTs for medication safety
questions.explain: OA is a clinical diagnosis. Inflammatory markers at low pre-test probability 'muddy the waters'. Safety labs (CBC, creatinine, LFTs, A1c) guide NSAID/acetaminophen choices. MRI doesn't change management; aspiration isn't needed for a cool, chronic knee.

questions.stem: A weight-bearing X-ray is taken of a 70-year-old's painful varus knee. Which set of findings is expected in osteoarthritis?
options: Non-uniform joint-space loss, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts
questions.explain: OA = LOSS: Loss of joint space (non-uniform, medial in varus), Osteophytes, Subchondral Sclerosis, Subchondral cysts. Osteopenia and marginal erosions suggest RA; syndesmophytes are SpA; metaphyseal bands suggest leukemia.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with knee OA has 10/10 pain limiting walking despite GLA:D physio, scheduled acetaminophen, topical diclofenac and a failed steroid injection. He is keen on surgery and can do rehab. What is the next best step?
options: Referral to orthopaedic surgery for total knee arthroplasty
questions.explain: Indications for TKA: QoL and function impaired, an adequate non-surgical trial has failed, he wants surgery, and he is fit for surgery and rehab. Arthroscopic debridement has no proven benefit in OA; repeating a failed injection or starting opioids is not appropriate.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old asks about knee replacement results. Which statement matches the counselling taught in CBL 39?
options: About 85% are satisfied, but 20–30% have ongoing pain; infection is about 1%
Infection occurs in about 1 in 5 cases
Implants last a lifetime, so earlier is better
questions.explain: ~85% improve, but 20–30% have persistent pain; periprosthetic infection is ~1%; death <1%. Implants last ~15–20 years, so very young patients face revisions (harder: scar, altered anatomy). Aseptic loosening is a common late complication.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old has 8 weeks of intermittent low back pain aggravated by bending forward and sitting, relieved by extension. No leg symptoms, no red flags, and a normal neuro exam. What is the most likely underlying pathology?
options: Herniated disc compressing a nerve root
questions.explain: Back-dominant, flexion-aggravated pain = Pattern 1, most often discogenic. Pattern 2 (extension-aggravated) = facets; Pattern 3 (constant leg pain + neuro signs) = herniation; Pattern 4 (leg pain walking, relieved sitting) = stenosis (WFQ).

questions.stem: A 42-year-old has 2 weeks of constant low back pain radiating down the left leg to the foot and can't work. There are no red flags and no neurological deficit. What is the best next step?
options: Positions of relief, simple analgesics and gentle exercise
Opioids and 5 days of bed rest
questions.explain: First-line is conservative: positions of comfort (Z-lie, prone on pillows), an NSAID ± a neuropathic agent (the course's CORE Back Tool strikes out acetaminophen), and activity as tolerated. Imaging and referral come if it doesn't improve, deficits appear or red flags emerge. Bed rest and first-line opioids are not recommended (WFQ).

questions.stem: A 30-year-old has acute back pain with constant right leg pain to the toes, new lateral calf paresthesia, and now feels she always needs to urinate but passes only a little each time. Which finding most strongly suggests cauda equina syndrome requiring urgent surgical assessment?
questions.explain: Urinary retention (followed by insensible overflow), fecal incontinence and saddle numbness define cauda equina syndrome, a surgical emergency. Check a post-void residual (>50–100 cc abnormal), saddle sensation and rectal tone, and get an urgent MRI.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old with a history of IV drug use has 3 days of back pain that wakes him at night, with fevers. Morning stiffness lasts 15 minutes. Bladder and bowel are normal. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explain: NIFTI: fever + IV drug use = infection (discitis, osteomyelitis, epidural abscess) → X-ray and MRI. SpA needs >3 months of insidious inflammatory pain; 15 minutes of stiffness and 3 days' duration don't fit (WFQ).

questions.stem: Which of these patients most clearly warrants referral to a spine surgeon?
options: 72-year-old with progressive neurogenic claudication despite physiotherapy
52-year-old with a second disabling episode of acute back-dominant pain
28-year-old with 3 months of persistent back-dominant pain
questions.explain: Surgical criteria: failure of ≥12 weeks of compliant conservative care, unbearable constant leg pain, expanding deficits, recurrent disabling sciatica, or disabling neurogenic claudication. Back-dominant pain alone is not a surgical indication, and 2 weeks is too early (WFQ).

questions.stem: A 34-year-old developed non-radiating low back pain 7 days ago. She is otherwise well, has tried to stay active, but feels she isn't progressing and wants more help. Which referral is most appropriate?
questions.explain: Early mechanical back pain without red flags → physiotherapy for pattern-specific exercise and self-management. One week is far too short for inflammatory back pain (>3 months), and surgeons or physiatrists come after conservative care fails (WFQ).

questions.stem: A 78-year-old has bilateral leg pain after walking 2 blocks. He can walk for 30 minutes leaning on a shopping cart and cycles without pain. Pedal pulses are normal. What best explains his symptoms?
options: Neurogenic claudication from lumbar spinal stenosis
questions.explain: Neurogenic claudication (Pattern 4) is positional: flexing the spine (shopping cart, bicycle) opens the canal and relieves it. Vascular claudication depends on muscle demand, so the distance is the same whatever the posture. Manage with flexion exercises and sitting breaks; surgery if disabling.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old with 8 weeks of low back pain believes bending will 'damage his spine', has stopped all activity, and expects massage and injections to fix him. What do these features represent, and what is the priority?
options: Yellow flags; education and reassurance to reduce the risk of chronicity
questions.explain: Yellow flags: belief that pain is harmful, fear-avoidance, low mood and withdrawal, and expectation of passive treatment. They predict chronic pain; address them with education, reassurance, active rehab ± CBT (Keele STarT Back, PHQ-4).

questions.stem: A patient with neck pain is being assessed. Which finding indicates the need for an urgent MRI of the cervical spine?
options: New difficulty with fine motor tasks in the hands
Tingling medial to the shoulder blade
Pain in the middle finger of one hand
Pain radiating to the suboccipital region
questions.explain: New clumsiness or fine-motor difficulty suggests cervical myelopathy (cord compression), along with gait imbalance, bilateral numbness and hyperreflexia, and warrants an urgent MRI and surgical evaluation (WFQ).

questions.stem: A 72-year-old has 6 months of neck pain, 3 months of bilateral hand numbness, leg weakness and falls. He has a wide-based gait, can't tandem walk, and has upper- and lower-limb hyperreflexia with a positive Babinski. What is the best treatment?
questions.explain: This is cervical myelopathy: UMN signs in all four limbs, gait disturbance and hand numbness. It needs surgery. Manipulation is dangerous. Never diagnose bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome until cord pathology is excluded.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old has constant arm-dominant pain radiating to the middle finger. Extension with rotation and axial loading of the neck toward that side reproduces the arm pain, and manual traction relieves it. The triceps reflex is reduced. Which root is most likely affected?
questions.explain: Positive Spurling's + relief with distraction = cervical radiculopathy. C7: middle finger dermatome, triceps myotome and triceps reflex. C6 = thumb/biceps; C8 = little finger/finger flexion; C5 = shoulder/deltoid.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old data-entry clerk has 12 months of intermittent posterior neck, upper back and bilateral shoulder pain that improves on vacation. There is diffuse posterior muscle tenderness; range, strength and neuro exam are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explain: Intermittent, work-related pain that improves away from work, with diffuse muscle tenderness and a normal exam = postural pain. A cuff tear would weaken abduction; OA limits range; disc disease would give dominant neck pain or root signs (WFQ).

questions.stem: A 25-year-old has had recurrent low back pain since age 18. Sitting for any length of time is uncomfortable, sustained exercise lessens the pain, and there are no fevers. What X-ray finding would you most expect?
questions.explain: Young onset, chronic, worse with rest and better with exercise = inflammatory back pain of axial SpA. Enthesitis drives osteoblastic new bone: syndesmophytes bridging vertebrae and SI sclerosis/erosions/fusion (WFQ).

questions.stem: A 20-year-old university student has aching low back pain. Which history feature would most raise your suspicion of inflammatory back disease?
options: Swelling at the back of his left heel for 2 months
It worsens after running and hockey
Shooting pain down his left leg to the foot
questions.explain: Posterior heel swelling = Achilles enthesitis, an extra-articular feature of SpA. Three weeks is too short (IBP >3 months), pain after exercise is mechanical, and shooting leg pain is radicular/neuropathic (WFQ).

questions.stem: In which of these patients would an X-ray of the sacroiliac joints best help diagnosis?
options: 38-year-old ICU nurse with back pain on most workdays
20-year-old with 3 weeks of back pain after hockey
28-year-old with long-standing back pain, stiff when getting up at night to feed her baby, better once moving
50-year-old with psoriasis whose back is sore climbing stairs
questions.explain: Long-standing pain that is worse with rest (night stiffness) and better with activity is inflammatory, and such patients often have sacroiliitis visible on X-ray. Pain with work, sport or stairs is mechanical, even in someone with psoriasis (WFQ).

questions.stem: A 29-year-old with ankylosing spondylitis (axial disease only) has persistent inflammatory back pain despite two full-dose NSAIDs over 3 months. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explain: For axial SpA: NSAIDs first, then biologics (TNF-α or IL-17 inhibitors). Conventional synthetic DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine) don't help spinal disease; they're used for peripheral-only SpA. Screen for TB first.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old with 6 months of mechanical-sounding back pain and no SpA features asks for an HLA-B27 test 'to be sure'. What is the best response?
options: Order it: a negative result rules out AS
Don't order it without specific SpA features: sensitivity and specificity are limited (about 1 in 50 carriers develop AS)
Order it with RF and ANA as a screen
questions.explain: HLA-B27 is associated with axial SpA but has limited sensitivity and specificity, so order it only at moderate pre-test probability, and don't repeat past results (Choosing Wisely). It is not a monitoring test.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl had a viral illness last week and now limps with groin pain but can bear weight. She is afebrile and her bloodwork is normal. You diagnose transient synovitis of the hip. What is the most appropriate medication?
questions.explain: Transient synovitis (age 3–10, post-viral, afebrile) is treated with NSAIDs. It is a diagnosis of exclusion: septic arthritis (fever, non-weight-bearing, high WBC/ESR) needs aspiration, IV antibiotics and orthopaedics. Steroids could mask infection (WFQ).

questions.stem: A 3-year-old with a painful right hip refuses to bear weight for 3 days after an URI. Temperature 39.1°C, WBC 15,500, ESR 55. How many Kocher criteria does he meet, and what is the next step?
options: 4 (~99% probability of septic arthritis); urgent aspiration, blood cultures and orthopaedics
questions.explain: Kocher: non-weight-bearing, fever >38.5°C, WBC >12,000, ESR >40: all four, ~99.6% probability of septic arthritis. That is a surgical emergency: joint aspiration + blood cultures, OR washout, then IV antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl has calf pain before bed most nights that resolves by morning. She is otherwise healthy with no fever, swelling, limp or activity limitation, and her exam is normal. What is the best next step?
questions.explain: Classic growing pains (age ~3–12, bilateral, evening, no red flags, normal exam) → watch and wait. Investigate only if pain persists or red flags appear (WFQ).

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl has 2 months of fatigue, 10 kg weight loss, pallor, easy bruising and joint aches that wake her at night, with no joint swelling. Knee X-rays show metaphyseal lucent bands. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explain: Night pain, constitutional symptoms, bruising, pallor, weight loss and metaphyseal bands without effusions = leukemia. Get a CBC and blood film (blasts), then bone marrow biopsy, and refer urgently to oncology (WFQ).

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl has 3 months of bilateral hand swelling and stiffness. She is otherwise well, with no fever or rash. She has synovitis of both wrists, right MCP2–3 and left MCP3–4. How is her JIA classified?
questions.explain: Six joints (≥5), small and large, in a young girl = polyarticular JIA. Oligoarticular involves ≤4 mostly large joints (knee); systemic has quotidian fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, organomegaly and serositis (WFQ).

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl has 2 months of a swollen left knee and a stiff right ankle with an effusion; ANA is positive. Besides NSAIDs and intra-articular steroid injections, which intervention is essential?
options: Screening eye exams every 3–6 months for asymptomatic uveitis
questions.explain: Oligoarticular JIA (young girl, ≤4 large joints, ANA+ ~80%) carries a high risk of asymptomatic uveitis (risk: girls, young onset, oligo, ANA+), so screen every 3–6 months. Other complications: leg-length discrepancy, contractures, wasting, TMJ disease, growth problems.

questions.stem: A 2.5-year-old has daily spiking fevers with an evanescent rash during the fevers, neck and hip arthritis, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and a pericardial rub. Hb 80, CRP 250. After NSAIDs and prednisone fail, which targeted therapy is most appropriate?
questions.explain: Systemic JIA: quotidian fever, rash with fever, lymphadenopathy, HSM, serositis. Escalate quickly: NSAIDs → prednisone → IL-1 (anakinra) or IL-6 inhibition. In the module, fever, rash and arthritis resolved within 5 days of anakinra.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old tennis player with chronic right shoulder pain feels sudden severe pain while serving and now cannot initiate abduction. Ultrasound shows a full-thickness rotator cuff tendon tear with an effusion. Which muscle is most likely torn, and what is its primary function?
questions.explain: The supraspinatus inserts on the greater tubercle, initiates abduction and is the tendon most often torn or impinged under the coracoacromial arch. Teres minor externally (not internally) rotates. Confirm a tear with MRI, the most sensitive test.

questions.stem: Aspirated shoulder fluid is cloudy with 25,000 WBC/µL (neutrophils) and a negative Gram stain. Under polarized light with a red compensator, rhomboid crystals appear blue when parallel to the compensator axis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explain: Rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals, blue when parallel = CPPD. Gout crystals are needle-shaped, strongly negative, yellow when parallel and often intracellular. Hydroxyapatite isn't seen on routine microscopy.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old falls 6 feet onto an outstretched hand: dorsal wrist deformity, median-nerve numbness, positive Tinel's at the carpal tunnel. X-rays show dorsal dislocation of the carpus relative to the lunate and a carpal fracture. Which bone is fractured, and why the median nerve findings?
options: Scaphoid; the displaced carpus compresses the carpal tunnel contents
questions.explain: A trans-scaphoid perilunate fracture-dislocation. Displacement narrows the carpal tunnel, compressing the median nerve. Urgent closed reduction, then OR (scaphoid screw, K-wires, carpal tunnel release) if reduction fails or neuro deficits persist.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old on hydrochlorothiazide develops a hot, swollen elbow with firm nodules and numbness and weakness of the ring and little fingers. Aspirate shows needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent intracellular crystals. Where is the nerve most likely compressed?
options: Cubital tunnel behind the medial epicondyle
questions.explain: Gouty olecranon bursitis (tophi, thiazide) compresses the ulnar nerve as it passes behind the medial epicondyle through the cubital tunnel. Tests: Froment's and Wartenberg's signs. Ulnar paradox: clawing is worse with a low lesion because FDP still works.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old falls on an outstretched arm. The elbow is swollen and tender; X-ray shows a raised anterior lucency (sail sign) without an obvious fracture line, and POCUS shows an elevated posterior fat pad. What do these findings indicate?
options: An elbow joint effusion (hemarthrosis), suggesting an occult fracture
questions.explain: The fat pads are displaced by an intra-articular effusion: the anterior 'sail' on X-ray, an elevated posterior fat pad on POCUS. After trauma this implies hemarthrosis/lipohemarthrosis and an occult fracture. Imaging MSK trauma always starts with plain films.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old with CKD (creatinine 200) has a febrile, red, hot right knee for 5 days. Aspirate: 65,000 WBC (80% PMN), needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals, culture negative. What is the best acute treatment?
questions.explain: Gout confirmed with infection excluded. NSAIDs are contraindicated in CKD; colchicine works only within 12–36 h and is poorly cleared in renal disease; an intra-articular steroid is preferred over oral in monoarthritis. Acetaminophen doesn't treat the inflammation.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman has 3 months of hip, then shoulder and neck, pain with 1 h of morning stiffness, 10 lb weight loss, painful but normal-strength muscles, Hb 108, platelets 450, ESR 60, CRP 72, and normal CK and TSH. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explain: PMR: age >50, girdle pain and stiffness, constitutional symptoms, high ESR/CRP, anemia, thrombocytosis, no weakness, normal CK. Not myositis (painless weakness, high CK), not fibromyalgia (normal labs), not RA (wrong joints).

questions.stem: A 26-year-old has gradually worsening widespread pain, all-day stiffness, fatigue and tenderness everywhere, with no swollen joints and give-way weakness from pain. Which initial blood tests are most appropriate?
questions.explain: Basic bloodwork excludes fibromyalgia mimics (hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism/hypercalcemia, systemic illness). Avoid ANA, RF and HLA-B27 at low pre-test probability: false positives cause harm (WFQ).

questions.stem: A 38-year-old has 10 days of back-dominant, flexion-aggravated low back pain with no red flags and normal kidney function. According to the course's CORE Back Tool, what is the first-line medication?
questions.explain: The course's edited CORE Back Tool strikes out acetaminophen for Patterns 1, 2 and 4 and leaves an NSAID; Rampersaud: acetaminophen "can work but is not as effective". Opioids are reserved for severe Pattern 3 pain; muscle relaxants aren't recommended for non-specific LBP.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old with chronic low back pain now reports numbness and clumsiness in both hands and a new unsteady gait. Where is the lesion most likely?
questions.explain: Neurological dysfunction flows downstream: a lumbar lesion never causes hand symptoms, but a cervical lesion can cause hand and gait symptoms (myelopathy). Don't diagnose bilateral carpal tunnel until the cord is excluded.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old with constant leg-dominant pain from an acute disc herniation asks whether he needs surgery. What proportion of disc herniations improve without surgery?
questions.explain: Rampersaud: 80–90% of disc herniations improve without surgery. Pattern 3 is the one pattern where medication comes first so the patient can move; relief with rest positions makes surgery less likely.

questions.stem: On a modified Schober test, marks are placed at the PSIS line and 10 cm above it. On full forward flexion the distance increases to 13 cm. How do you interpret this?
questions.explain: A normal increase is ≥5 cm; an increase of 3 cm is abnormal (reduced lumbar flexion). The test is non-specific (ascites or a large abdomen also limit it) but raises the pre-test probability of axial SpA.

questions.stem: In which condition are NSAIDs considered disease-modifying?
questions.explain: Dr. Yang: NSAIDs are not disease-modifying in RA or other seropositive disease, but in axial SpA they are: "NSAIDs are only a DMARD for axial SpA". csDMARDs don't work for the spine; biologics come next.

questions.stem: Which statement about uveitis in JIA is correct?
options: It is usually a red, painful eye in oligoarticular JIA
It is silent in oligo- and polyarticular JIA, so children need regular eye screening
It never occurs in enthesitis-related arthritis
questions.explain: In oligo and poly JIA the uveitis is asymptomatic, so every child is screened (every 3–6 months in oligo JIA, more often if ANA+). In ERA, as in adult SpA, it presents as a red, painful eye.

questions.stem: Which bedside test specifically checks median nerve motor function in the hand, as taught in the MAPS case?
options: The OK sign: a round O made by thumb IP and index DIP flexion
questions.explain: The OK sign tests FPL (thumb IP flexion) and index FDP (DIP flexion). A flat pad-to-pad pinch doesn't test the median nerve. Froment's and Wartenberg's are ulnar signs; Finkelstein's tests De Quervain's.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old has 6 weeks of neck-dominant mechanical pain with a normal neuro exam. Which intervention does the CORE Neck Tool list as NOT recommended?
questions.explain: For acute neck-dominant pain the tool recommends reassurance, independent exercise and an NSAID, with active therapy if needed. Rest/immobilization, cervical collars, neck pillows, electrical modalities and relaxation massage are not recommended.

cards.prompt: How does OARSI define osteoarthritis, and what is it NOT?
cards.answer: A disease of synovial joints representing failed repair of joint damage from joint-level or systemic stresses on all joint tissues (synovium, subchondral bone, cartilage, ligaments, menisci), leading to cartilage and bone breakdown. It is not an inevitable part of aging or simple wear and tear.

cards.prompt: List the joint-level risk factors for OA.
cards.answer: Obesity/BMI (load), joint injury (ACL tear, meniscal tear or resection), limb malalignment (varus/valgus), abnormal bone shape (e.g. hip dysplasia), and neuromuscular abnormalities (weakness, neuropathy, poor proprioception).

cards.prompt: List the systemic risk factors for OA.
cards.answer: Aging (reduced chondrocyte repair, bone turnover, sarcopenia), female sex (~2× disabling OA), genetics (~50% of hand/hip OA; high bone density), and obesity (adipokines: hand OA risk ~2×).

cards.prompt: Why is OA considered a serious disease?
cards.answer: Loss of function and disability (especially walking), impact on comorbidities (60–90% have another condition; more diabetes and CVD from sedentary behaviour), and premature mortality (mostly cardiovascular).

cards.prompt: Which factors inside and outside the joint drive OA pain?
cards.answer: Inside/around the joint: synovitis, effusion, cartilage defects, muscle weakness. Outside: genetics, sleep disturbance, depression, pain catastrophizing, and central sensitization.

cards.prompt: What are the four key questions in non-traumatic knee pain?
cards.answer: 1) Inflammation (local or systemic)? 2) Malignancy red flags? 3) Referred from elsewhere (lower lumbar spine, hip)? 4) Anatomy: where is the pain (anterior, medial, lateral, posterior)?

cards.prompt: How is a meniscus tear managed?
cards.answer: Non-surgically first: physio, NSAIDs, activity modification. Over 50% resolve by 8–12 weeks, although tears rarely heal. MRI if not better at 3 months. Surgery (repair or resection) if conservative care fails or QoL is impaired.

cards.prompt: List early and late complications of arthroplasty.
cards.answer: Early local: infection, neurovascular injury. Early systemic: mortality, transfusion, cardiac events, stroke, DVT/PE, pneumonia. Late: prosthesis failure (aseptic loosening), persistent pain, stiffness, revision surgery.

cards.prompt: What are the core OA treatments appropriate for all patients?
cards.answer: Exercise/physical activity, weight management, and self-management/education (e.g. the Arthritis Society programs). Exercise is the most effective non-surgical treatment.

cards.prompt: Outline the stepwise drug approach to OA.
cards.answer: First local: topical NSAID, topical capsaicin. Then systemic: acetaminophen, oral non-selective NSAID or COX-2 selective NSAID (+ GI protection). Additional: intra-articular corticosteroid, duloxetine. Opioids generally not appropriate.

cards.prompt: How do you give an adequate trial of acetaminophen for OA?
cards.answer: 1000 mg per dose (two Extra Strength) on a regular schedule, e.g. BID, for at least 2 weeks, within the daily maximum (tutor used 3 g/day), checking for duplicate acetaminophen products. 'Stay on top of the pain instead of chasing it.'

cards.prompt: Why are opioids discouraged in knee OA?
cards.answer: Adverse effects, tolerance and misuse; the knee won't improve, so you commit the patient to opioids until arthroplasty and then face a difficult wean ('what's your endgame?').

cards.prompt: Why are oral NSAIDs a poor choice for Mr. H (70, T2DM nephropathy, HTN on ramipril, sulfa allergy)?
cards.answer: Nephropathy + ACE inhibitor (AKI, hyperkalemia), hypertension (NSAIDs raise BP), age 70 (Beers; GI bleed). Celecoxib, the usual GI-sparing option, contains a sulfonamide, so it's out with his sulfa allergy.

cards.prompt: When should a patient with knee OA be referred for arthroplasty?
cards.answer: When symptoms significantly impair QoL and function, an adequate trial of recommended non-surgical therapy has failed, the patient is medically fit and can do post-op rehab, benefits outweigh risks, and the patient wants surgery.

cards.prompt: How does physical activity lower blood glucose, short and long term?
cards.answer: Short term: contraction-driven, insulin-independent GLUT4 translocation (AMPK), glycogen resynthesis, more muscle blood flow, insulin sensitivity for 24–48 h. Long term: more GLUT4, better PI3K/Akt signalling, more muscle mass, weight loss, less visceral fat and inflammation.

cards.prompt: List the CORE Back Tool history questions.
cards.answer: 1) Where is your pain worst (back vs leg)? 2) Constant or intermittent? 3) What increases your typical pain? 4) What can't you do now that you could before, and why? 5) Any unexpected bladder/bowel accidents? 6) If onset <45, morning stiffness >30 min?

cards.prompt: What does NIFTI stand for, and what investigation goes with each?
cards.answer: Neurological (progressive deficit, cauda equina) → urgent MRI; Infection (fever, IVDU, immunosuppression) → X-ray + MRI; Fracture (trauma, osteoporosis) → X-ray ± CT; Tumour (cancer history, weight loss, night pain) → X-ray + MRI; Inflammation (>3 months, onset <45, stiffness >30 min) → rheumatology.

cards.prompt: List the yellow flags for chronic back pain.
cards.answer: Belief that back pain is harmful or severely disabling; fear and avoidance of movement; low mood and social withdrawal; expectation of passive treatments rather than active participation.

cards.prompt: What are the criteria for surgical referral in low back pain?
cards.answer: Failure of ≥12 weeks of compliant conservative care; unbearable constant leg-dominant pain; worsening nerve-tension signs; expanding motor, sensory or reflex deficits; recurrent disabling sciatica; disabling neurogenic claudication; suspected cauda equina (urgent). Back-dominant pain alone is not an indication.

cards.prompt: Distinguish myelopathy from radiculopathy.
cards.answer: Myelopathy: dysfunction of the spinal cord from compression ('sick cord'): bilateral clumsy hands, gait imbalance, hyperreflexia, Hoffman/Babinski, ± bladder. Radiculopathy: compression of one nerve root causing pain, numbness or weakness in its dermatome/myotome.

cards.prompt: What questions screen for cervical myelopathy (DOWN)?
cards.answer: Dropping things or clumsy hands? Off-balance or unsteady on your feet? Weakness in one or both arms/hands? Numbness or tingling in arms/hands? 3 of 4 is highly suspicious (image and refer), but the lecturer treats any one positive (starting after the neck pain) as a concern. Dropping things and imbalance are the early signs.

cards.prompt: List the features of inflammatory back pain.
cards.answer: Onset <45 (ASAS IBP criteria: <40), insidious, >3 months, morning stiffness >30 min, better with exercise, worse with rest, night pain in the second half of the night (better on getting up), alternating buttock pain, very responsive to NSAIDs.

cards.prompt: How does treatment differ between axial and peripheral-only SpA?
cards.answer: All: education, exercise, PT, analgesia. Any axial disease: NSAIDs, then biologics (TNF-α or IL-17 inhibitors). Peripheral only: csDMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, leflunomide), then biologics or tsDMARDs (e.g. upadacitinib).

cards.prompt: List the red flags in a child with limb pain or limp.
cards.answer: Fever, pain waking from sleep, lethargy, redness, non-weight-bearing, poor growth/weight loss, pinpoint tenderness, trauma, morning stiffness (inflammatory).

cards.prompt: Define juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
cards.answer: Arthritis with onset before age 16, lasting ≥6 weeks, with other causes excluded (idiopathic). There is no diagnostic test. Arthritis = effusion, or ≥2 of pain/tenderness on movement, limited motion, warmth.

cards.prompt: What are the complications of oligoarticular JIA?
cards.answer: Asymptomatic uveitis (screen every 3–6 months), flexion contractures, muscle wasting, leg-length discrepancy (overgrowth of the affected leg), TMJ disease, and growth disturbance.

cards.prompt: What features suggest leukemia in a child with limb pain, and what tests do you order?
cards.answer: Night pain, constitutional symptoms (lethargy, weight loss, night sweats), bruising, pallor, hepatosplenomegaly, often no effusions; metaphyseal bands on X-ray. Order CBC and blood film (blasts), LDH/urate, then bone marrow biopsy; refer urgently to oncology.

cards.prompt: What should be done with aspirated synovial fluid?
cards.answer: Record gross appearance (volume, colour, clarity, viscosity); cell count and differential; Gram stain and culture; crystal analysis under polarized light; ± chemistry (glucose, protein, LDH) and cytology. Give clinical details on the requisition.

cards.prompt: How is a trans-scaphoid perilunate dislocation with median nerve symptoms managed?
cards.answer: Urgent closed reduction under sedation and neurovascular reassessment. If it fails, is unstable, or neuro symptoms persist: urgent open reduction and fixation (scaphoid headless compression screw, K-wires) plus carpal tunnel release.

cards.prompt: What is the ulnar paradox?
cards.answer: Clawing of the ring and little fingers is worse with a LOW (wrist) ulnar lesion than a HIGH (elbow) lesion: with a low lesion FDP is still innervated and pulls the fingers into flexion unopposed by the paralysed intrinsics.

cards.prompt: Distinguish PMR, inflammatory myositis and fibromyalgia on exam and labs.
cards.answer: PMR: girdle pain/stiffness, no weakness, high ESR/CRP, normal CK. Myositis: painless proximal weakness, high CK, antibodies, MRI/EMG. Fibromyalgia: widespread pain and diffuse tenderness, normal exam and labs.
