guides.title: Week 39 · 1 Osteoarthritis: Pathogenesis, Risk Factors & Burden
guides.html:
OA · Pre-week

Osteoarthritis: Pathogenesis, Risk Factors & Burden

Week 39 · MSK III — OA, Spine & Pediatric Rheumatology
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

OA as failed repair of the whole joint, the joint-level and systemic risk factors, why it is a serious disease, and why pain and X-ray don't match.

What OA is (and isn't)

OA is not an inevitable part of aging or simple "wear and tear". It is "a disease of synovial joints that represents failed repair of joint damage resulting from joint-level or systemic stresses on the joint tissues (synovium, subchondral bone, cartilage, ligaments, menisci) → breakdown of cartilage and bone" (OARSI). All joint tissues are involved: the field has moved away from a cartilage-only view. The OA knee (Hunter 2011 figure) shows cartilage breakdown, bone remodelling and sclerosis, osteophytes, meniscal damage, synovial hypertrophy, ligament dysfunction, muscle atrophy and altered fat metabolism.

The model: joint-level factors (loading, biomechanics) and systemic factors converge on cartilage matrix destruction → a failed attempt at repair → mechanical failure of the joint → joint destruction.

OA is less a single entity than a final common pathway of many causes (genetic, developmental, metabolic, traumatic). Unlike inflammatory arthritis, structural change (the disease) and symptoms (the illness) correlate imperfectly.

Language (CBL 39)
U of T rheumatologists object to "wear and tear" because normal wear shouldn't cause OA; the mechanism is failed repair. The CBL tutor admitted she still uses it with patients as shorthand for "non-inflammatory".

Joint-level risk factors (altered loading → focal damage)

FactorKey facts
Obesity (BMI)Magnitude of joint load. Raises knee and hand OA risk (women > men). ~5 kg weight loss ≈ 50% lower risk of knee OA
Joint injuryMeniscal tear/partial meniscectomy → 4–6× knee OA risk. ~50% have knee OA 10–20 years after an ACL tear (ACL tears ~1.5× more common in women). No evidence surgical repair prevents OA
MalalignmentVarus/valgus unbalances load (varus → medial compartment)
Bone shapeE.g. hip dysplasia
NeuromuscularMuscle weakness/wasting, neuropathy, poor proprioception

Normal load-bearing depends on menisci (distribute load, act as spacers so ligaments don't go lax) and the ACL (prevents anterior translation/medial rotation of the tibia).

Systemic risk factors

  • Aging: higher bone turnover (reduced bone mass, subchondral fractures); chondrocytes less able to repair, so the articular surface softens and the matrix loses tensile strength and stiffness; sarcopenia; slower reactions (injury).
  • Sex: women are ~2× as likely to have disabling OA (hormones, body shape, genetics, social determinants).
  • Genetics: hand and hip OA are familial (~50% genetic); high bone density raises knee/hip risk. Early hand OA often follows a maternal family history.
  • Obesity works systemically too: hand OA risk is ~2× higher with obesity even though hands don't bear weight, via systemic adipokines from adipose tissue (the lecture's example is the infrapatellar fat pad). Adipokines (leptin, adiponectin, visfatin, resistin) act on chondrocytes, which then release inflammatory mediators (NO, IL-6, IL-8, MCP-1) and cartilage-degrading enzymes (MMPs, ADAMTS-4/5). The CBL tutor grouped obesity, HTN, T2DM and gout together as metabolic risk that raises susceptibility.
Most important modifiable risk factor for knee OA = increased body mass (WFQ).

OA is a serious disease

  • Prevalence: 1 in 8 adults (1 in 5 by age 70); the most common arthritis; women > men; ~95% of joint replacements are for OA.
  • Disability: a leading cause of years lived with disability; OA rose from 15th (1990) to 11th (2010) in the Global Burden of Disease ranking, a 64% increase in years lived with disability. Hip/knee OA is the biggest contributor to walking difficulty (hand OA reduces grip). Quality of life 10–25% lower; limits on daily and valued activities (ADLs, sport/leisure, work), loss of independence, social isolation, depression.
  • Comorbidity: 60–90% have at least one other condition (HTN, diabetes, CVD, depression). OA raises the incidence of diabetes (and diabetes complications) and CVD, largely through sedentary behaviour from walking limitation.
  • Mortality: symptomatic hip/knee OA is linked to reduced survival, mostly cardiovascular.
  • Symptoms drive the burden: pain ↔ depressed mood, poor sleep, fatigue, central sensitization → disability and restricted participation.

Pain in OA (SLM02)

  • Pain (IASP): "an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage, or described in terms of such damage". Chronic pain: pain that persists or recurs beyond the inciting injury.
  • Pathway: nociceptor → peripheral nerve → dorsal horn → ascending tracts → cortex; descending pathways can inhibit or enhance it.
  • Central sensitization: abnormal pain transmission leading to a state of pain amplification.

OA pain is classically nociceptive, but central sensitization contributes in some people, and the individual's pain mechanism guides treatment. Chronic OA pain is a disease in its own right, best understood through a biopsychosocial framework. These factors change the severity, duration and localization of pain: pain that spreads beyond the joint suggests drivers outside it.

In and around the jointOutside the joint
Synovitis, effusion, cartilage defects, periarticular muscle weaknessGenetics, sleep, depression, pain catastrophizing

Why X-ray and pain don't match: X-ray shows only bone changes (sclerosis, cysts, osteophytes) and infers cartilage loss from joint-space narrowing. MRI adds soft tissue but gives no information on biopsychosocial factors or nociception. Treat the patient, not the film.

Key message (PW03): the many pathways to OA are an opportunity for a personalized approach, targeting treatment to the specific cause (e.g. malalignment, obesity).

OA = failed repair of the whole joint. Joint-level: obesity, injury (ACL/meniscus), malalignment, shape, weakness. Systemic: age, female sex, genes, obesity (adipokines). A serious disease: disability, comorbidity, earlier death. Pain has intra- and extra-articular drivers, so imaging can't explain it.

guides.title: Week 39 · 2 Approach to Non-Traumatic Knee Pain
guides.html:
SLM01 · Knee

Approach to Non-Traumatic Knee Pain

Week 39 · MSK III — OA, Spine & Pediatric Rheumatology
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Four key questions, pain by location, meniscus tear vs OA, and the knee exam findings the CBL tutor corrected.

Four key questions

  1. Inflammation? Systemic (fever, chills, other joints) or local (warmth, effusion, morning stiffness) → septic, crystal, inflammatory arthritis.
  2. Malignancy red flags? Anorexia, weight loss, masses, symptoms of a primary, past/family history of cancer → X-ray, MRI, primary workup.
  3. Referred? Most often from the lower lumbar spine (back pain, radicular pattern, sensory change, weakness, neuro findings) or the hip (groin pain, limited and irritable internal rotation). Always examine the hip.
  4. Anatomy: where is the pain? Anterior, medial, lateral or posterior.

Pain by location

SiteConditionFeatures and management
PosteriorBaker's cystPopliteal synovial cyst from posterior herniation of synovium secondary to an effusion (OA, meniscus tear). Rarely symptomatic unless it ruptures (posterior knee and calf pain). Acute: rule out DVT. Chronic: treat the cause of the effusion
AnteriorPatellofemoral pain syndromeRetropatellar pain without intra-articular pathology; young, active, female; squatting, kneeling, sitting, sport. Physio, orthotics, NSAIDs, activity change, taping
MedialPes anserinus syndromeSartorius, gracilis, semitendinosus + bursa; tender ~5 cm below the joint line; overuse, obesity, OA, malalignment. Local symptom control, activity modification
LateralIliotibial band syndromeOveruse friction over the lateral femoral condyle with repetitive flexion/extension; snapping, local tenderness, maximal pain at ~30° flexion. Symptomatic management
Medial/lateralStress fractureNormal bone, repeated normal force (activity–fitness mismatch); female sex, nutrition. X-ray, MRI; rest, symptomatic management, physio, titrated return to activity; casting for resistant cases
Intra-articularMeniscus tear, OASee below. The meniscus (fibrocartilage) acts as a shock absorber; the articular cartilage creates a friction-free surface (SLM01)

Meniscus tear vs osteoarthritis

Meniscus tearOsteoarthritis
AgeYoungerOlder
OnsetAcute, traumatic (twist, pivot)Chronic, insidious
CourseWorst at onset, improves, often resolves within ~3 monthsMild at first, progressive
AggravatingSquatting, pivotingProlonged standing and walking; better with rest
AssociatedMechanical clicking, locking, instability, swellingCrepitus
SignsEffusion, meniscal provocation tests, point tendernessMalalignment, flexion contracture, crepitus, general joint-line tenderness
InvestigationMRI if not better in 3 monthsX-ray (SLM01; the CBL adds that it often isn't needed to diagnose)
WFQ traps
Acute onset makes OA less likely; a normal X-ray or absent effusion doesn't. A confirmed meniscal tear in a 42-year-old with no treatment yet → physiotherapy first (not arthroscopy, bracing or complete rest).

Treatment

  • Meniscus tear: non-surgical first (physio, NSAIDs, activity modification). >50% resolve by 8–12 weeks, but tears rarely heal. Surgery (arthroscopic repair vs resection) only if conservative care fails or QoL suffers. Younger patients and high-level athletes are the surgical group.
  • OA arthroplasty (replacement or resurfacing) when pain is significant and disabling, QoL is impaired, conservative care has failed, and benefit outweighs risk. Success ~80% (SLM; the CBL tutor quoted ~85% satisfied). Counsel on activity expectations afterwards.
  • Arthroplasty complications. Early local: infection, neurovascular injury. Early systemic: death, transfusion, cardiac events, stroke, DVT/PE, pneumonia. Late: prosthesis failure, revision.

Knee exam pearls from CBL 39

  • Articular vs periarticular: the best discriminator is limited active AND passive movement (periarticular problems hurt actively but keep passive range), plus joint-line tenderness and swelling of the joint itself rather than a bursa.
  • Crepitus is a poor discriminator (almost everyone has it). An effusion doesn't tell you articular vs periarticular either.
  • Bulge sign positive = SMALL effusion. Moderate–large effusions: bulge negative, ballottement positive; very large: patellar tap. The first sweep counts.
  • Varus ("varus my horse": knees out) is the classic OA deformity, because the medial compartment carries most load, narrows first, then snowballs.
  • Hands: Heberden (DIP), Bouchard (PIP), CMC1 squaring. Nodes are bony and asymmetric; effusions are soft and symmetric.
Knee pain: inflamed? malignant? referred (hip, L-spine)? where? Meniscus = young, acute twist, locking, point tenderness → physio first, MRI at 3 months. OA = older, insidious, activity pain, crepitus. Bulge sign = small effusion. Baker's cyst rupture: rule out DVT.

guides.title: Week 39 · 3 Non-Surgical Management of Osteoarthritis
guides.html:
OA · Treatment

Non-Surgical Management of Osteoarthritis

Week 39 · MSK III — OA, Spine & Pediatric Rheumatology
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Core treatments for everyone, how to actually prescribe exercise, the stepwise drug ladder, why oral NSAIDs and opioids are usually wrong in older adults, and what not to use.

The treatment pyramid

LevelWhoTherapies
Core (base)All patientsExercise, weight management, self-management/education (Arthritis Self-Management Program)
LocalManyTopical NSAIDs, topical capsaicin, intra-articular corticosteroid
SystemicWorsening symptomsAcetaminophen, oral NSAIDs (± GI protection) or COX-2 inhibitors, duloxetine
SurgeryFewJoint replacement

Risk of adverse effects rises as you climb. Individualize by number of joints, comorbidities (contraindications), and patient preference.

OARSI (knee OA)No comorbidityWith comorbidity
RecommendedBiomechanical interventions, IA corticosteroid, topical NSAIDs, topical capsaicin, acetaminophen, oral NSAIDs (non-selective + GI protection, or COX-2), duloxetineBiomechanical interventions, IA corticosteroid, topical NSAIDs and topical capsaicin (knee), oral COX-2 inhibitors, duloxetine. Acetaminophen and non-selective NSAIDs drop out of this column

Note the tension with CBL 39, where scheduled acetaminophen is the tutor's first systemic step in a comorbid older adult.

Exercise: the most effective non-surgical treatment

  • Definitions: physical activity = any bodily movement by skeletal muscle that uses energy; exercise = regular activity done to improve or maintain fitness or health; exercise therapy = a regimen designed and prescribed for specific therapeutic goals (restore MSK function, reduce pain).
  • All international guidelines recommend exercise therapy. Largest effect on symptoms with the lowest risk of serious harm (WFQ answer); benefits are independent of radiographic severity and baseline pain, so every OA patient can be offered it.
  • Effect sizes (pain / function; ≥0.2 small, ≥0.5 moderate, ≥0.8 large): exercise ~0.6 / 0.58; NSAID (ibuprofen) ~0.44 / 0.35; acetaminophen ~0.18 / 0.16; education ~0.23 / 0.06 and weight loss ~0.2 / 0.23 (small, but without serious adverse events, unlike the drugs).
  • How it works: it reduces physical impairments (deconditioning, weakness and lean-mass loss, stiffness, excess weight and joint load, poor balance/falls) and metabolic alterations (hyperglycemia, lipids, excess adipose tissue, AGE accumulation, systemic inflammation).
  • Prevents functional loss, reduces pain, aids weight loss, and manages HTN, CVD and diabetes.
  • Targets: 150 min/week moderate–vigorous activity. The biggest mortality gain is getting sedentary people moving (≤75 min/week gives ~20% risk reduction). ~6000 steps/day protects against functional limitation. Severe knee OA can tolerate a starting dose of ~70 min/week of walking.
  • Therapeutic exercise via PT: quadriceps strengthening, ROM, balance/proprioception, neuromuscular training. Tai chi, aquatics, walking, "any exercise they like" (pickleball in a brace counts). Increase walking by about 10% a week and split long walks into shorter ones. Ankle weights or a weighted vest don't damage the joint by definition: try them if they aren't painful (CBL tutor).
  • Pain during exercise is allowed: the lecture allows a rise of no more than 2–3/10, and its scale shows 0–2 safe, 2–5 acceptable, >5 high risk; GLA:D likewise accepts up to ~5/10. Pain should settle within 24 h. Hurt is not harm, and walking does not damage the knee.
  • Prescribe it like a drug: frequency, duration, reps, a buddy, functional goals. The CBL tutor's substitute when physio is unaffordable is a printed knee-exercise handout (she named OrthoInfo, from the AAOS), 2–3×/week for 15 min.

Weight and self-management

  • As little as 5% weight loss reduces pain and disability and systemic inflammation. Diet + exercise beats either alone. Raise it gently, with permission.
  • Self-management programs: pain down ~20%, physician visits down ~40%, less depression and disability. Arthritis Society (arthritis.ca): education, support, and the Arthritis Rehabilitation and Education Program (free PT/OT guidance).
  • GLA:D: a structured education + supervised exercise program for knee/hip OA, run with orthopaedics and often recommended before surgery (CBL tutor: physio 3×/week for 8 weeks; the published protocol is 2 education + 12 exercise sessions over ~6 weeks). It can prevent the need for surgery.
  • Physio access in Ontario: cost is the barrier (needs insurance; OHIP clinics have long waits). Cane in the contralateral hand. Braces only sparingly: constant use weakens the quadriceps, and "if you're at the point where you always need the brace, you're gonna be thinking about surgery".

Drugs, stepwise

StepDrugNotes
1 LocalTopical NSAID (diclofenac), topical capsaicin (OARSI: knee)Minimal systemic exposure: first-line in older adults and with comorbidity. Topical diclofenac comes in regular and extra strength, and a stronger compounded version exists
2 SystemicAcetaminophenGive a real trial: 1000 mg per dose, scheduled, for 2 weeks. Tutor's ceiling 3 g/day, a conservative limit often used in older adults (her claim that the max was 'revised down' doesn't match the Canadian label, which remains 4 g/day for adults); check for duplicate products. 500 mg PRN is not a trial. Products: Extra Strength = 500 mg per tablet (so 1000 mg = two tablets); Tylenol Arthritis = 650 mg extended-release (label: 2 caplets every 8 h, max 6 a day; the tutor's regimen is 2 tablets twice a day). "Stay on top of the pain instead of chasing it"
2 SystemicOral NSAID or COX-2+ GI protection (PPI or misoprostol). Avoid in CKD, ACEi/ARB/diuretic users, CHF, HTN, anticoagulation, age >65 (Beers). Celecoxib is a sulfonamide: avoid in sulfa allergy
Add-onIntra-articular corticosteroidWeeks of relief; warn diabetics about transient hyperglycemia
Add-onDuloxetineEspecially with depression or widespread pain
AvoidOpioidsGenerally not appropriate (adverse effects, tolerance, misuse). "What's your endgame?" Once started you're committed until arthroplasty, then must wean
NSAIDs in the older patient
"Of 10 patients you see, 9 cannot take NSAIDs." Anticoagulant + NSAID is a hard stop (the tutor's figure: roughly 10–20× bleeding risk). HTN is the most common adverse effect; also AKI, edema, hyperkalemia, CHF, GI bleed, transaminitis, confusion/falls, urticaria, bronchospasm, and platelet inhibition (reversible; aspirin's is irreversible). Mechanism: COX inhibition blocks prostaglandins, including the ones that dilate the renal afferent arteriole, so ACE inhibitor + diuretic + NSAID is the "triple whammy" for the kidney. CV risk (MI, stroke) is highest with COX-2 selective drugs and diclofenac, lowest with naproxen. GI-bleed risk factors: age >65, prior ulcer, steroids, SSRIs, H. pylori. Interactions: anticoagulants, ACEi/ARB/diuretics, SSRIs, lithium, methotrexate. The tutor's story: 3 days of NSAID in a 73-year-old with pseudogout led to a massive GI bleed.

What not to use

Uncertain (lecture)Not recommended
Acupuncture, mineral baths, avocado-soybean unsaponifiables, rosehip, diacerein, glucosamine, intra-articular hyaluronic acid (knee; ACR 2019 conditionally recommends against it for the knee, per the CBL prep), ultrasound (knee)Chondroitin, risedronate, strontium; opioids generally; TENS and stem cells (ACR)

WFQ: glucosamine/chondroitin are generally not recommended (not clinically proven; placebo effect; unlikely harmful). PRP: rheumatology guidelines say no (preparation too variable); orthopaedic guidelines include it. Semaglutide improved knee OA pain in STEP 9 (whether directly or through the weight loss, "we don't really know", per the CBL tutor) but is not approved for OA (off-label, not covered); consider it when there's another indication.

The future (PW05): drugs with more effect and fewer adverse effects, disease-modifying OA drugs (DMOADs), and regenerative therapy (PRP, biologics, stem cells, tissue engineering). None is established yet.

Everyone gets exercise + weight + self-management; exercise is the single most effective therapy. Then topical NSAID, then properly dosed scheduled acetaminophen, IA steroid or duloxetine; oral NSAIDs only if no renal/CV/GI/anticoagulant risk. No opioids; chondroitin not recommended and glucosamine uncertain (WFQ: both generally not recommended). Always non-drug first, then drugs.

guides.title: Week 39 · 4 Knee OA in an Older Adult (CBL 39)
guides.html:
CBL · Mr. H

Knee OA in an Older Adult (CBL 39)

Week 39 · MSK III — OA, Spine & Pediatric Rheumatology
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Mr. H end to end: why it's articular and non-inflammatory OA, why no tests are needed, the X-ray LOSS findings, safe prescribing with comorbidities, and when a knee replacement is right.

The case

Mr. H, 70: HTN, T2DM with retinopathy and nephropathy, gout (one first-MTP attack 10 years ago), right ACL tear. On amlodipine, metformin, ramipril, acetaminophen 500 mg PRN. Sulfa allergy. ODB coverage. 5 years of bilateral knee pain, R > L, worse over the last month, with stairs and snow shovelling; settles with rest; clicking. BMI 85/1.65² = 31.2.

Exam: antalgic gait, bilateral varus, right knee mildly swollen, not red, lacks full extension; limited active and passive flexion, crepitus, joint-line tenderness, R bulge sign (small effusion), both knees cool, no laxity; CMC1 squaring + Heberden's nodes.

The history: what to ask (Q1)

  • Inflammatory vs non-inflammatory: morning stiffness duration, gelling, better or worse with activity, night/rest pain.
  • Mechanical symptoms in every OA patient: locking, catching and giving way.
  • In an older adult: PMR/GCA red flags (girdle stiffness, headache, jaw claudication, vision); gout history.
  • Function and fall risk; the actual acetaminophen dose taken; ideas, concerns and expectations.
  • Pain score (the one item the tutor added): the number matters less than what it tells you about impact, pain is what the patient says it is, and its real value is comparing visit to visit ("I've dropped their pain four points").

Articular, non-inflammatory, OA

  • Articular: limited active and passive range, joint-line tenderness, joint swelling, fixed flexion, varus.
  • Non-inflammatory: cool, not red, use-dependent pain relieved by rest, small effusion, bony (not boggy) swelling. The tutor's inflammatory list is swelling, warmth, redness, pain at rest improving with movement, and morning stiffness over 30–60 min. OA has synovitis at the tissue level; "non-inflammatory" describes the clinical pattern.
  • Diagnosis: bilateral medial-compartment knee OA, post-traumatic on the right (the old ACL injury altered biomechanics even though the knee is now stable), on a background of nodal hand OA. Risk factors: ACL, metabolic syndrome, age, genetics, varus.
  • Differential: gout (too chronic, cool knees), CPPD (can coexist; look for chondrocalcinosis), septic (afebrile, bilateral), late-onset RA, PMR, referred hip/L-spine, superimposed meniscal tear.

Investigations: none needed to diagnose

OA is a clinical diagnosis (age ≥45, activity-related pain, no or ≤30 min morning stiffness). Explain why no test is needed; an X-ray on request is not unreasonable, and films earn their place for surgical planning. Skip ESR/CRP at low pre-test probability (they "muddy the waters"), and remember a normal result wouldn't exclude inflammatory arthritis anyway (some people have a low baseline). Do order safety labs before drugs: CBC, creatinine/eGFR ± ACR, LFTs, A1c. MRI only for surgical questions, treatment failure, or unusual pathology (TB, PVNS, tumour).

X-ray findings of OA: "LOSS"

LetterFinding
LLoss of joint space, non-uniform (medial in varus)
OOsteophytes
SSubchondral sclerosis
SSubchondral cysts

Best taken weight-bearing; add a lateral, a skyline/Merchant view (patellofemoral joint) and a Rosenberg 45° PA view for early medial narrowing. No periarticular osteopenia or marginal erosions (those suggest inflammatory disease). Kellgren–Lawrence grades 0–4; severity correlates poorly with pain.

Arthrocentesis

Not needed here, but reasonable when injecting anyway, if the knee turns acutely hot (gout likes damaged joints), or when a treated RA/JIA patient has one mechanical-looking swollen knee. Send the 3 C's (+ cytology if oncologic concern). OA fluid: clear ("read newsprint through it"), straw-coloured, viscous (strings), WBC <2000. Never aspirate a prosthetic knee in clinic (ortho, sterile technique) and never posteriorly (neurovascular bundle).

  • "A single inflamed joint should almost always undergo at least one diagnostic aspiration" (NEJM video). Don't go through overlying cellulitis.
  • Technique (prep): 18-gauge needle; EDTA tube for the cell count, heparin tube for crystals; keep at least 5 cc for Gram stain and culture.
  • The knee cavity is continuous, so the suprapatellar/anterior approach usually drains a Baker's cyst too (or it settles after a steroid injection). Several knee bursae don't connect with the joint.

Why his knees lock and catch

Degenerate meniscal tear, cartilage loss, osteophytes, loose bodies, effusion (pseudo-locking), fixed flexion contracture. Mechanical symptoms prompt orthopaedic assessment, but arthroscopic debridement/meniscectomy has no proven benefit in OA.

Explaining the diagnosis (Q5)

Common and manageable; not an inevitable decline; movement is medicine (walking won't damage the knee); weight and strength are the levers he controls; a flare doesn't mean new damage. Check understanding with teach-back.

Management plan (non-drug first)

  1. Fix the acetaminophen: 1000 mg scheduled BID for a 2-week trial.
  2. Topical diclofenac.
  3. Exercise prescription building on his daily dog walk + quad/hip abductor strengthening; walking will not damage the knee.
  4. Arthritis Society / GLA:D; weight loss 5–10% raised with permission; cane in the left hand; brace only situationally.
  5. Consider an IA steroid (warn about glucose).
  6. Avoid oral NSAIDs: nephropathy + ramipril + HTN + age, and celecoxib is out because of his sulfa allergy. No opioids.

Exercise and blood sugar

Short term: contraction-driven GLUT4 translocation (AMPK, insulin-independent), glycogen resynthesis, more muscle blood flow, insulin sensitivity for 24–48 h. Long term: more GLUT4, better PI3K/Akt signalling, more muscle mass (a bigger glucose sink), weight loss, less visceral fat and inflammation.

Semaglutide and knee OA

STEP 9: in obese knee-OA patients, semaglutide 2.4 mg gave ~14% weight loss and larger WOMAC pain improvement than placebo, with less rescue analgesia. Caveats from the prep: the placebo arm (lifestyle counselling) also improved a lot; the trial population (82% female, mean age 56, mean BMI 40) is unlike Mr. H; 2.4 mg is the weight-loss dose, not the diabetes dose; adverse-event discontinuation 6.7% vs 3.0%. Not approved for OA; for Mr. H it's prescribed for diabetes, where GLP-1 agonists also bring renal (FLOW) and cardiovascular (SUSTAIN-6) benefit. Caveats: diabetic retinopathy (monitor; the signal came from SUSTAIN-6), gout flares with rapid weight loss, lean-mass loss (keep resistance training).

When to refer for knee replacement

Checklist
1. Symptoms negatively impact QoL and function (function, not X-ray grade, is the indication)
2. An adequate trial of recommended non-surgical therapy has failed (max analgesia, exercise/GLA:D, failed steroid injection)
3. Medically fit, and able to do post-op rehab
4. The patient wants surgery; benefits outweigh risks

Timing: implants last ~15–20 years, so avoid very young patients (repeated revisions) but don't wait until frailty prevents rehab. Optimize A1c before surgery (infection risk; the prep cites a target of <8%); surgical risk rises with BMI above ~35–40. Fitness concerns the tutor named: untreated severe OSA, anticoagulation, heart failure; in some patients (e.g. wheelchair-bound with bilateral Charcot feet) a knee replacement "may actually worsen things".

Before referring (prep): re-examine for a superimposed CPPD/gout flare, infection or referred hip/spine pain; consider aspirating the knee; check duloxetine was tried. Surgeons choose between unicompartmental (UKA) and total (TKA) replacement. Expectations are the strongest predictor of dissatisfaction.

TKA outcomes (tutor's figures)

  • ~85% satisfied/improved, but 20–30% have ongoing pain.
  • Early: periprosthetic infection ~1%, VTE, neurovascular injury, death <1%, MI, stroke, pneumonia, delirium.
  • Late: persistent pain, aseptic loosening, stiffness (poor rehab), revision. Revisions are harder: scar, altered anatomy, older patients.
  • Mortality: a student offered ~1 in 10,000 and the tutor agreed; spinal anaesthesia and nerve blocks make it safer than general anaesthesia.
  • Prep figures: symptomatic DVT ~1–2% with prophylaxis, PE <1%, stiffness needing manipulation under anaesthesia ~2–5%, peroneal nerve palsy and periprosthetic fracture each <1%.
  • Expect: flexion to about 110–120° (kneeling often stays difficult), numbness lateral to the incision; recovery 3–6 months with gains to ~12. Dissatisfaction is predicted by catastrophizing, depression, widespread pain and milder X-ray disease before surgery.

The tutor's closing theme: OA is mostly managed in family medicine, and "sometimes is harder to treat than rheumatoid arthritis": the tools are limited, so use each one properly.

Cool knees + bony swelling + joint-line pain + varus = OA; diagnose clinically, labs only for drug safety. X-ray = LOSS. Fix acetaminophen dosing first, topical NSAID, exercise, weight; no oral NSAIDs with CKD/ACEi/sulfa allergy, no opioids. TKA when function is impaired after failed maximal non-surgical care in a willing, rehab-capable patient.

guides.title: Week 39 · 5 Low Back Pain: CORE Back Tool
guides.html:
Spine · Lecture

Low Back Pain: CORE Back Tool

Week 39 · MSK III — OA, Spine & Pediatric Rheumatology
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

History-led pattern recognition, NIFTI red flags and yellow flags, cauda equina, the four patterns and their management, and when to refer.

Why a framework

70–80% of people get low back pain; 30–40% annual prevalence; the #1 cause of years lived with disability; 20–25% of sufferers have disabling pain, and 25% of patients account for 75% of the cost (more costly than cardiac disease and diabetes combined, per the lecturer). Imaging findings rarely correlate with symptoms: disc "wear" on MRI is the "grey hair of the spine", and the chance of an abnormal MRI roughly tracks your decade of life (degeneration in ~30% of asymptomatic people in their 20s, 60–70% by their late 50s). The approach is history, history, history, with exam and tests to confirm. The goal is restoring function and reducing (not necessarily abolishing) pain, with patient self-management.

CORE Back history questions

  1. Where is your pain the worst? Back/buttock-dominant (anywhere from the 12th rib to the gluteal fold) vs leg-dominant. If the answer is "everywhere": "Which pain limits your function?", "If I could take away one pain…", "Would you rather sit, stand or lie down?" (and watch whether they sit or stand during the interview). Pain patterns are dynamic.
  2. Constant or intermittent? (Does it ever fully stop?) Constant: rule out red flags.
  3. What increases your typical pain? Flexion vs extension vs walking/standing.
  4. What can't you do now? (and why): screens yellow flags; should match Q1.
  5. Any unexpected bowel or bladder accidents? Rule out cauda equina.
  6. If onset <45: morning back stiffness >30 min? Screen for inflammatory arthritis.

Red flags: NIFTI

FlagCluesInvestigation
NeurologicalDiffuse motor/sensory loss, progressive deficits, cauda equinaUrgent MRI
InfectionFever, IV drug use, immunosuppressionX-ray + MRI
FractureTrauma, osteoporosis risk, fragility fractureX-ray ± CT
TumourCancer history, unexplained weight loss, significant night pain, severe fatigueX-ray + MRI
Inflammation>3 months, onset <45, stiffness >30 min, better with exercise, night painRheumatology
The "downstream" rule (Rampersaud)
Neurological dysfunction flows top-down: a neck lesion can cause leg or balance symptoms, but lower back nerve compression never affects the upper limb. Hand symptoms mean the neck (or the brain: think stroke).
Non-mechanical pain (CORE Back)
If no mechanical pattern is identified, the pain is non-mechanical. Non-spine pain: consider other causes before pain medication, including referred pain from the kidney, uterus, bowel or ovaries. Spine pain that doesn't fit a pattern: consider centralized pain medications (antidepressants, anti-seizure drugs, opioids) and a pain disorder.
Cauda equina: surgical emergency
Urinary retention followed by insensible overflow, unrecognized fecal incontinence, distinct saddle/perineal numbness. In the young, usually a large central disc herniation. Check a post-void residual (>50–100 cc abnormal), saddle sensation and rectal tone. Ask about change since this episode, not long-standing symptoms.
Lecturer's pearls: insensate loss (no warning that they need to go) is neurological; urgency with not reaching the toilet in time is not. Altered or tingly saddle sensation is the early sign ("if they get complete loss, it's probably too late"); fecal incontinence comes last. When in doubt, image. Send them to the emergency department, not a routine surgical referral: caught early, recovery is "fantastic"; with full incontinence and lost rectal tone it is "50-50 at best and never complete". Teach Pattern 3 patients these warning signs.

Yellow flags (psychosocial risk of chronicity)

Belief that back pain is harmful or severely disabling; fear/avoidance of movement; low mood and social withdrawal; expectation of passive treatment rather than active participation. Ask at any visit, and specifically for pain >6 weeks or not responding to treatment; manage with education and reassurance ± CBT (Keele STarT Back, PHQ-4). About 50% of people with chronic pain have mood changes. A patient demanding surgery is itself a yellow flag. Exam signs of abnormal pain processing: widespread myofascial tenderness, allodynia (e.g. screaming at light touch), pain behaviour, the "doorbell sign".

Exam essentials

Minimum exam (CORE Back, bold on the tool): flexion/extension movement testing, patellar reflex (L3–4), great toe extension (L5), great toe flexion (S1), plantar response, passive SLR, saddle sensation (S2–4). Full list: gait, heel walk (L4–5), toe walk and repeated toe raises (S1), Trendelenburg (L5), flexion/extension movement testing, passive hip range of motion (supine: joint above/below; if hip movement reproduces the pain, the hip is the likely source), prone passive back extension (patient uses the arms to lift the upper body), patellar reflex (L3–4), quadriceps (L3–4), ankle dorsiflexion (L4–5), EHL (L5), FHL (S1), ankle reflex (S1), plantar response/UMN signs, passive SLR, femoral stretch (L3–4), gluteus maximus (S1), saddle sensation (S2–4). Referred leg pain has a normal neuro exam; radicular pain gives a +SLR (reproduces leg pain) ± deficits. Dermatomes: L3 anterior thigh, L4 shin, L5 top of foot/big toe, S1 back of calf/sole. Sitting stretches the nerve like an SLR; the Z-lie relieves it because the bent knee slackens the sciatic nerve. Palpation: a tender muscle points to sprain/strain; Pattern 1 pain that isn't tender is probably discogenic.

The four patterns

PatternFeaturesLikely sourceManagement
1 Back-dominant, flexion-aggravatedBending, sitting, driving hurt; constant or intermittent; normal neuro. Most common; younger patients. Faster response if prone extension helpsDisc / soft tissueLimit sitting to ~30 min, lumbar roll, walking breaks; extension exercises (prone press-ups: lecture 10 reps × 2 sets, 3–5×/day; CORE tool 10 reps 3×/day); NSAID. Follow up 2–4 weeks (PRN if a home program works); self-management once pain is reduced
2 Back-dominant, extension-aggravatedStanding, walking, leaning back hurt; intermittent; normal neuro. Older patients (facet arthritis)Facet joint arthritisFoot stool, sitting breaks, avoid overhead reach, cycling; flexion exercises (prayer stretch, knee-to-chest; CORE tool: sit, bend forward, push back up with hands on knees); NSAID. Follow up 2–4 weeks; self-management from session 1–2
3 Leg-dominant, constantRadiating below the knee; flexion-aggravated but all movements typically hurt; +SLR ± sensory/motor/reflex deficit. Young (20s–40s), the most painful patternDisc herniation pinching a nerve rootThe one pattern where medication comes first (pain control enables movement): NSAIDs ± neuropathic agent (pregabalin), opioids if first-line isn't enough; position of comfort 30 min every hour (Z-lie, prone on pillows); exercise aggravates it, so start with pain-relieving positions; change positions often. 80–90% of disc herniations improve without surgery; relief with rest positions makes surgery less likely. Imaged earliest (if not improving, or before an intervention/surgery). Follow up at 2 weeks (pain and neuro review); not usually suited to self-management
4 Leg-dominant, intermittentBrought on by walking/standing (extension), relieved by sitting/leaning forward; normal neuro at rest. Older (often in their 80s)Spinal stenosis: neurogenic claudicationFlexion exercises, sitting breaks, cycling, walker or Nordic poles; NSAID; surgery if disabling. Follow up 6–12 weeks (symptoms and functional impact)

If both directions hurt, find the neutral mid-range and limit the extremes; over-correction can flip the painful direction.

Neurogenic vs vascular claudication
Neurogenic is positional: better when the spine flexes (leaning on a shopping cart, cycling). Vascular claudication depends on muscle demand, not position: the calf hurts at the same distance whatever the posture (a stenosis patient can sit on a bike without pain). Many Pattern 4 patients are in their 80s and can have both: absent pulses or cold feet push vascular disease up the list, so work up both (spine imaging + vascular ultrasound).

Management principles and what not to do

  • Reassure (LBP usually settles but often recurs), stay active, modify activity by directional preference ("hurt vs harm"), return-to-work plan, self-management. Imaging doesn't help acute or recurrent LBP without red flags; follow up if symptoms last >6 weeks.
  • First-line analgesia is an NSAID (unless contraindicated: GI bleed history, renal disease, hypertension, older age). The course's edited CORE Back Tool strikes out acetaminophen for Patterns 1, 2 and 4, and the lecturer said acetaminophen "can work but is not as effective". Topical creams help muscular pain. Key message: "It is activity, and not the medication, that will help you recover more quickly." A new back pain of 7 days that isn't improving needs a physiotherapist (WFQ), not a surgeon or rheumatologist.
  • Bed rest is harmful ("the worst thing we ever designed medically": more disability, slower recovery). Bad care also means over-reliance on passive treatment and handing over an exercise sheet with no instruction. Patients with mild neurological symptoms should still do supervised rehab, moving in the direction that feels better; profound weakness needs a surgeon.
  • WHO 2023 (chronic primary LBP), recommended: structured education/advice (the #1 recommendation in every guideline), structured exercise, needling/acupuncture, spinal manipulation, massage, operant therapy and CBT, NSAIDs, topical cayenne (capsicum), multicomponent biopsychosocial care.
  • Not recommended (lecture slide, non-specific LBP): traction, therapeutic ultrasound, TENS, lumbar braces; opioids, SNRI/tricyclic antidepressants, anticonvulsants, muscle relaxants, glucocorticoids, injected local anesthetics; herbal remedies; pharmacologic weight loss. The same lecture still suggests pregabalin for pattern 3 radicular pain. (For neck-dominant pain, the CORE Neck Tool allows a short muscle-relaxant course only in acute pain and lists TCA/SNRI/antiepileptics for chronic pain; see the neck guide.)

Referral criteria

ReferralCriteria
Rehabilitation (4–12 treatments)No red flags; pain controlled enough to tolerate treatment; a mechanical directional preference; patient ready to be an active partner in goals and self-management
Pain management (criteria from the CORE Neck Tool; the Back Tool lists pain specialists only under specialist referral)Recommended options tried with reasonable compliance for ≥4 weeks, plus either high constant pain interfering with function or escalating/high-dose opioids. For limb-dominant pain, pain physicians can try nerve blocks first
Specialist optionsPhysiatry, CBT, pain specialist, multidisciplinary pain clinic, rheumatology; imaging and labs only for red flags

Surgical referral criteria

Failure of ≥12 weeks of compliant evidence-based conservative care; unbearable constant leg-dominant pain; worsening nerve-tension signs; expanding motor/sensory/reflex deficits; recurrent disabling sciatica; disabling neurogenic claudication; suspected cauda equina or myelopathy (urgent). Back- or neck-dominant pain alone is not an indication for surgery.

Ask: where worst, constant or intermittent, what aggravates, what can't you do, bladder/bowel, stiffness if <45. NIFTI. Pattern 1 flexion (disc) → extension exercises; 2 extension (facet) → flexion; 3 constant leg + neuro (herniation); 4 walking leg pain relieved by sitting (stenosis). Refer surgically for limb-dominant or neurological problems, not back pain alone.

guides.title: Week 39 · 6 Neck & Arm Pain: CORE Neck Tool
guides.html:
Spine · Cervical

Neck & Arm Pain: CORE Neck Tool

Week 39 · MSK III — OA, Spine & Pediatric Rheumatology
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Neck- vs arm-dominant pain, the myelopathy screen you must never skip, radiculopathy tests, root levels, red flags and management.

History

  1. Headache with the neck pain? Treat the headache first (headache navigator).
  2. Where is the pain worst? Neck-dominant (sub-occipital, trapezius, paraspinal, parascapular), arm-dominant (distal to the deltoid: upper arm, forearm, hand), or shoulder (deltoid, anterior shoulder: do a full shoulder exam).
  3. Constant or intermittent? Intermittent neck pain is mechanical and exercise-responsive. Judging "intermittent" needs an alert, non-medicated patient who can confirm a complete absence of pain, however brief; if that's hard to establish, rule out red flags. Intermittent arm pain: the CORE Neck Tool calls it referred (from neck or shoulder), not root pain, but Rampersaud's cervical Pattern IV is intermittent arm-dominant pain from foraminal stenosis in an older patient. Know both. Constant pain: rule out red flags and assess neuro status.
  4. Chest pain, dizziness or breathlessness? Consider a cardiac cause (and carotid dissection).
  5. Myelopathy screen (below).
  6. Trauma? Apply C-spine imaging rules; check for concussion.
  7. If ≤60, neck morning stiffness >30 min? Inflammatory arthritis screen.
  8. What can't you do now? Yellow flags.

Cervical myelopathy: don't miss it

Myelopathy = a "sick spinal cord" from compression; radiculopathy = compression of a single nerve root with dermatomal/myotomal symptoms.

DOWN questionnaire (≥3 of 4 = highly suspicious → image)
Dropping things / clumsy hands · Off-balance, unsteady gait · Weakness in arms/hands · Numbness or tingling in arms/hands.
Exam: wide-based gait, can't tandem walk, hyperreflexia, Hoffman's, Babinski, clonus (>3–4 beats), spasticity; ± bladder/bowel dysfunction. New difficulty with fine motor tasks warrants an urgent MRI of the C-spine (WFQ). Don't diagnose bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome until cervical cord pathology is excluded. Treatment is surgical decompression. Dr. Yang (ISAL): cervical myelopathy is an emergency the same way cauda equina is; consult surgery as soon as there are symptoms. The mJOA (modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association) score helps surgeons judge urgency.
Note: the CORE Neck Tool recommends surgical evaluation if any one of new gait change, fine-motor difficulty or new arm paresthesia is present, and the lecturer said a positive answer to any one DOWN question (if it began after the neck pain) is a concern, so 1–2 positives are not reassuring. Dropping things and imbalance are the early, subtle signs; weakness and numbness come later.

Red flags (NIFTI, neck version)

FlagCluesTest
NeurologicalCord compression, demyelination, progressive deficitsMRI
InfectionFever, meningism, immunosuppression, IV drug useX-ray + MRI
FractureOsteoporosis, trauma/fallX-ray ± CT
TumourCancer history, weight loss, night pain, fatigueX-ray + MRI
InflammatoryRA, PMR, GCARheumatology

Also examine the cervical lymph nodes (infection or tumour).

Neurological exam: root levels

RootMyotomeReflexDermatome
C4Trapezius (shrug)—Trapezius area
C5DeltoidBiceps (C5–6)Over the shoulder
C6BicepsBiceps (C5–6)Thumb, radial forearm
C7TricepsTricepsMiddle finger
C8Finger flexion (3rd digit)—Little finger, ulnar forearm
  • Observe gait and neck posture; record cervical AROM (flexion, extension, rotation, side flexion) with the pain it produces as a baseline for treatment response. The whole exam takes ~5 minutes.
  • Spurling's compression test (sitting): reproduces arm-dominant radicular pain (the lecturer skips it if active neck movement already reproduces the pain). Cervical distraction test (supine): positive if it relieves arm pain. Patients often find relief by supporting or elevating the arm (hand on head), which unloads the plexus and roots: the upper-limb equivalent of the Z-lie.
  • UMN screen: plantar response, Hoffman's; tandem gait if myelopathy is suspected.
  • Check shoulder range; if abnormal, do a full shoulder exam (shoulder pathology often coexists or mimics).

Cervical patterns (not validated)

Neck-dominantArm-dominant
I: constant, flexion-aggravated (discogenic; younger)
II: intermittent, extension-aggravated (facet OA; older)		III: constant radicular (herniated disc): in a young patient, "a cervical disc herniation until you prove otherwise"
IV: intermittent (foraminal stenosis; older)
Must rule out myelopathy

Management

  • General: posture correction, ergonomics, exercises opposite to the aggravating direction. Key messages: movement and activity reduce pain; imaging doesn't help acute or recurring neck pain without signs of serious pathology; follow up if symptoms last >6 weeks.
CORE Neck matrixNeck-dominantArm-dominant
Acute (<3 months): non-drugReassure (good prognosis); independent stretch, strengthening and aerobic exercise; active therapy if that fails (may include short-term mobilization/manipulation, endurance and balance work, short-term mechanical traction). 1–6 sessionsRelieving positions (arm abduction, supported elevation), frequent rest positions, manual/mechanical traction
Chronic (>3 months): non-drugMultimodal, goal-directed therapy; therapeutic clinical massage; low-level laser. 6–12 sessionsAs acute, plus a trial of acupuncture
DrugsStart with an NSAID (acetaminophen is struck out in the course version). Acute: short-course muscle relaxant (e.g. cyclobenzaprine, a few weeks). Chronic: TCA (amitriptyline, nortriptyline), SNRI (duloxetine, venlafaxine), antiepileptics (topiramate, pregabalin, gabapentin)NSAID; opioids for select patients; TCA/SNRI; antiepileptics (carbamazepine, gabapentin, pregabalin); acute only: muscle relaxant (~2 weeks) and, for severe radiculopathy, methylprednisolone or dexamethasone for 5–7 days (caution with infection or brittle type 1 diabetes)
Not recommendedAcute: rest/immobilization, cervical collars, neck pillows, electrical modalities, relaxation massage. Chronic: relaxation therapy/massage, electro-acupuncture, strengthening in isolation, mechanical/manual traction; SSRIs, glucocorticoids for mechanical pain, muscle relaxantsCollars, electrical modalities and relaxation massage have no proven effect. Topical NSAIDs: inconclusive

Referral (CORE Neck)

  • Surgical: failed ≥12 weeks of compliant conservative care; intolerable constant arm-dominant pain; worsening Spurling's; expanding motor, sensory or reflex deficits; suspected myelopathy (urgent).
  • Pain management: options tried with reasonable compliance for ≥4 weeks plus high constant pain interfering with function or escalating/high opioid doses. Options: pain specialist; multidisciplinary clinic (CBT, OT, activity-based) for chronic neck-dominant pain; interventional clinic with cervical epidurals for arm-dominant pain.
  • Rehab: the same four readiness criteria as the back tool.
  • Yellow flags for the neck add catastrophizing, unrealistic expectations of treatment, and the Pain Self-Efficacy Questionnaire (PSEQ) alongside the PHQ-4.
WFQ pattern: postural shoulder pain
A 32-year-old data-entry clerk with 12 months of intermittent posterior neck/upper back/shoulder pain that improves on vacation, diffuse muscle tenderness, and normal range, strength and neuro exam → postural pain (not a cuff tear, disc disease or OA).
Neck vs arm dominant; intermittent arm pain = referred (CORE Neck) or foraminal stenosis (Rampersaud Pattern IV). NSAID first, no collars. Always screen myelopathy (DOWN: dropping, off-balance, weakness, numbness) + hyperreflexia/Hoffman/Babinski → urgent MRI and surgery. Spurling reproduces radicular arm pain; distraction relieves it. C6 thumb, C7 middle finger/triceps, C8 little finger.

guides.title: Week 39 · 7 Inflammatory Back Pain & Spondyloarthritis
guides.html:
Lecture · Yang

Inflammatory Back Pain & Spondyloarthritis

Week 39 · MSK III — OA, Spine & Pediatric Rheumatology
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

How to spot inflammatory back pain, the axial vs peripheral SpA patterns, extra-articular clues, when to order HLA-B27 and imaging, and how treatment differs from RA.

The spondyloarthritis family

"Seronegative" (a historical term: RF and ANA negative) = spondyloarthritis (SpA): ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, IBD-associated arthritis, reactive arthritis, undifferentiated SpA. They share chronic inflammation of the spine, joints, eye, bowel and skin and the genetics of HLA-B27. About 1% of Canadians have SpA.

Predominantly axial: ankylosing spondylitis and other axial SpA (spine and SI joints). Predominantly peripheral: reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, IBD-associated arthritis, undifferentiated SpA (these can also involve the spine). The umbrella label lets you diagnose and start treatment at the first visit before the subtype is clear. (Seropositive, by contrast: RA, SLE, inflammatory myositis, systemic sclerosis, Sjögren's, MCTD.)

Rheumatoid arthritisAnkylosing spondylitis
Primary lesionSynovitisEnthesitis
Bone responseErosion and bone lossOsteoblast-driven new bone: syndesmophytes, bony fusion

Inflammatory back pain (axial SpA)

FeatureInflammatory back pain
Age of onset<45 (the ASAS IBP criteria use <40)
OnsetInsidious
Duration>3 months
Morning stiffness>30 min
ExerciseImproves
RestWorsens (sitting is uncomfortable)
Night painYes, second half of the night; better on getting up
Buttock painAlternating
NSAIDsVery helpful

Lumbar spine and SI inflammation is not a feature of RA or other seropositive disease. Inflammatory neck pain can occur in SpA (and in RA). Only <10% of back pain is inflammatory: 3 weeks of pain, pain after hockey or running, or shooting leg pain all point elsewhere.

Examination

  • Normal curves: cervical lordosis, thoracic kyphosis, lumbar lordosis, sacral kyphosis. Late AS fuses the spine irreversibly: exaggerated thoracic (and cervical) kyphosis (can't look ahead while walking, hard to lie flat) with loss of lumbar lordosis (a flat back that stays flat on forward flexion). Cervical fusion makes checking blind spots when driving hard.
  • Movements: cervical (flexion, extension, lateral flexion, rotation); thoracic (rotation, chest expansion); lumbar (modified Schober, lateral flexion). Track them over time.
  • Modified Schober: patient stands, feet hip-width apart; mark the line joining the PSIS (dimples of Venus) and a point 10 cm above it in the midline; patient bends forward fully with knees straight; re-measure. Normal = an increase of ≥5 cm; <5 cm is abnormal. Non-specific (ascites or a large abdomen also restrict flexion), but a positive test raises the pre-test probability of axial SpA.
  • FABER test (Flexion, ABduction, External Rotation): ipsilateral buttock/low back pain suggests sacroiliitis.

Peripheral SpA pattern

Asymmetric, oligo- or polyarticular, can involve DIPs, ± spine and SI joints. (Axial SpA doesn't involve peripheral joints; RA is symmetric and spares DIPs, lumbar spine and SI joints.)

Extra-articular clues

FeatureDetails
EnthesitisAnterior chest wall, pelvic brim, Achilles (heel swelling), plantar fascia; axial and peripheral SpA, never seropositive disease
DactylitisWhole-digit "sausage" swelling from inflammation of the whole tendon sheath plus the joints in between; more common in PsA; not seen in seropositive disease
EyeAnterior uveitis (most common EAM in AS: red painful eye, photophobia); conjunctivitis (reactive). Up to 42% of AS patients have an EAM: uveitis ~51%, psoriasis ~20%, IBD ~19%
Bowel / GUIBD; urethritis; GI or GU infection 1–4 weeks before reactive arthritis
Skin / nailsPsoriasis, nail pitting, onycholysis, oil-drop sign (PsA); erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, oral ulcers (IBD)

Investigations (only at moderate pre-test probability)

  • ESR/CRP: raised in up to ~75% but can be normal; if raised, a poor prognostic sign. Non-specific (infection also raises them).
  • RF/ANA: don't order them for purely axial disease or "just inflammatory back pain"; order only with peripheral arthritis when RA or lupus is on the differential (they should be negative).
  • HLA-B27: associated with axial SpA but limited sensitivity and specificity (only ~1 in 50 carriers develops AS). Don't order without specific SpA features, and don't repeat past results. Dr. Yang's use case: inflammatory back pain with normal X-rays; a positive B27 raises the probability enough to justify an MRI.
  • X-ray: SI joints (erosions, sclerosis, partial then complete fusion); lumbar/cervical spine (syndesmophytes = bony bridging). Grading is not examinable.
  • MRI: shows active, reversible inflammation (bone marrow edema) and chronic damage. Use it when history/exam suggest SpA but X-rays are normal, or when it's unclear whether inflammation persists on treatment.
  • No diagnostic criteria: diagnose from a compatible picture plus investigations. From a 5% baseline in chronic back pain, probability rises with IBP, heel enthesitis, peripheral arthritis, dactylitis, acute anterior uveitis, family history, a good NSAID response, raised ESR/CRP, HLA-B27, and sacroiliitis on MRI or X-ray (the likelihood ratios aren't examinable).
  • Average delay to diagnosis in AS: 9 years, because inflammatory back pain goes unrecognized. Primary care should recognize it and refer to rheumatology; early recognition prevents irreversible fusion.

Management

PatternTreatment
All patientsEducation, exercise, physical therapy, analgesia (oral agents or SI joint steroid injections)
Any axial diseaseNSAIDs first, then biologics (TNF-α or IL-17 inhibitors). csDMARDs don't work for the spine. In axial SpA NSAIDs are considered disease-modifying; in RA and other seropositive disease they are not ("NSAIDs are only a DMARD for axial SpA")
Peripheral onlycsDMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, leflunomide), then biologics or tsDMARDs (e.g. upadacitinib)
End-stageSurgery (e.g. hip replacement)

Scope (ISAL): you don't need the names of the biologics or targeted synthetic DMARDs, or the differences between the drug families, at this level.

Lecture quiz answers
AS: back pain that improves with physical activity. A 40-year-old with buttock pain worse at rest, night waking, a psoriatic plaque and DIP4, wrist and ankle swelling → psoriatic arthritis. Joint-pattern quiz: A = RA (symmetric peripheral, sparing SI and lumbar spine); B = PsA (asymmetric peripheral + spine and SI); C = first-MTP monoarthritis, most likely gout.
IBP: onset <45, insidious, >3 months, stiffness >30 min, better with exercise, worse at rest, second-half-of-night pain, alternating buttock pain, NSAID-responsive. SpA clues: enthesitis (heel), dactylitis, uveitis, psoriasis/nails, IBD, recent infection. X-ray: sacroiliitis, syndesmophytes; MRI if X-ray normal. Axial = NSAID → biologic.

guides.title: Week 39 · 8 The Limping Child & Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis
guides.html:
SLM04 · Pediatrics

The Limping Child & Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

Week 39 · MSK III — OA, Spine & Pediatric Rheumatology
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Red flags in a child with joint pain, septic arthritis vs transient synovitis (Kocher), leukemia and growing pains, and the JIA subtypes with their complications and treatment.

Red flags in a child with limb pain

Fever · pain waking from sleep · lethargy · redness · non-weight-bearing · poor growth/weight loss · pinpoint tenderness · trauma · morning stiffness. Red flags mean urgent investigation.

Inflammatory painNon-inflammatory pain
Swelling, erythema, warmth, AM stiffness, NSAID-responsive; exam: contracture, muscle wastingWidespread pain, family history of pain, less response to therapy, pain out of proportion; exam normal or discordant

Differential of the limping child

CategoryExamples
TraumaInjury (including non-accidental)
InfectionSeptic arthritis, osteomyelitis, viral (parvovirus), reactive/post-infectious, transient synovitis
NeoplasmBone tumour; leukemia, lymphoma, neuroblastoma
MechanicalHip AVN (Legg–Calvé–Perthes), SCFE, overuse
AutoimmuneJIA, SLE, dermatomyositis, IgA vasculitis (HSP)
HematologicHemophilia, sickle cell anemia
OtherPain syndromes (e.g. fibromyalgia), hypermobility/overuse, psychogenic pain (older children: the "mind–body connection"), growing pains

JIA is a diagnosis of exclusion within this differential.

Septic arthritis vs transient synovitis

Septic arthritis is a surgical emergency: fever, redness, swelling, refusal to bear weight. Send to the ED/orthopaedics for joint aspiration + blood culture, usually OR washout; empiric antibiotics after cultures; admission and prolonged IV antibiotics. The more WBCs and neutrophils in the fluid, the more likely it is septic.

Kocher criteria (septic hip vs transient synovitis)
1) Non-weight-bearing · 2) Fever >38.5°C · 3) WBC >12,000/mm³ · 4) ESR >40 mm/h (or CRP >20 mg/L; the SLM slide's "mg/dL" is a unit error).
Probability of septic arthritis: 0/4 = 0.2% · 1/4 = 3% · 2/4 = 40% · 3/4 = 93% · 4/4 = 99.6%.

Transient synovitis: benign inflammation of the hip capsule, ages 3–10, boys > girls, limp and hip/groin pain days to weeks after a viral illness, afebrile at presentation. The child appears well and not irritable, with normal WBC, ESR and CRP; the infection is "done and dusted". A diagnosis of exclusion. Treat with NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen); not antibiotics, and not steroids (if it were septic, steroids would stop the immune system fighting the infection: WFQ). Dr. Rozenblyum noted transient synovitis and reactive arthritis also affect the knees, not only the hips.

Malignancy (leukemia)

Weeks of limp and leg pain, pain waking at night, constitutional symptoms (lethargy, weight loss, night sweats), bruising, pallor, hepatosplenomegaly, often no effusions. Order CBC and blood film (blasts), LDH/urate; X-ray may show metaphyseal bands. Confirm with bone marrow biopsy; refer urgently to oncology.

Growing pains

Ages ~3–12 (SLM; 3–10 in the summary lecture); bilateral calf/thigh/shin pain at night before bed, normal between episodes, no morning stiffness or activity limitation, normal growth, exam and labs. May occasionally wake the child or cause a limp, but no other red flags. Watch and wait with reassurance; investigate if it persists or new features appear. Unrelated to growth; children outgrow it.

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

  • Juvenile: onset <16. Idiopathic: other causes excluded. Arthritis lasting ≥6 weeks. No diagnostic test. The most common chronic arthritis of childhood (~1 in 1000). Polyarticular JIA and RA are told apart only by age of onset (<16 vs >16); the JIA label usually stays into adulthood.
  • Workup to exclude mimics (SLM04 case): CBC, ESR/CRP, LDH/urate, X-ray, autoantibodies, and TB and Lyme testing. ANA isn't needed for the diagnosis but risk-stratifies uveitis: ANA+ children are screened more often.
  • JIA is often not very painful: children are stiff and achy but keep using the limb, unlike an "excruciatingly painful" septic joint.
  • Arthritis = joint swelling/effusion, or ≥2 of tenderness/pain on movement, limited movement, warmth (hips show limited range rather than swelling).
Subtype (share)FeaturesKey points
Oligoarticular (~50%; SLM 50–60%)≤4 joints; age <5, girls; large joints, knee most common; ANA+ ~80%, RF−. Oligo-persistent stays at ≤4 joints; oligo-extended later becomes polyarticular (managed the same way)Asymptomatic uveitis: screening eye exams every 3–6 months. NSAIDs ± IA steroid injections (very effective) + physio; poor response → add methotrexate
Polyarticular (~25% in the summary lecture; SLM 30–35%)≥5 joints, small and large (hands); girls; RF− (~20%, often younger children) or RF+ (~5%: older girls, symmetric, nodules, RA-like); ANA+ ~50%; uveitis 10–20%NSAIDs ± injections → methotrexate → biologics (etanercept, infliximab, adalimumab); earlier if severe. Check C-spine, growth, eyes
Systemic (~15% on the summary slide; SLM 10–20%)Daily spiking fevers (well between spikes, not chronically unwell), an evanescent salmon-pink rash in heat areas (axillae, groin) that comes with the fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, serositis, arthritisBone marrow biopsy first to exclude a hidden malignancy, then NSAIDs → prednisone → rapid escalation to IL-1 (anakinra) or IL-6 inhibition
Psoriatic (~5%; SLM 2–15%)Psoriasis + arthritis; can present with dactylitis or nail changes (pitting, onycholysis) without the rash
Enthesitis-related (~5%)Older boys; hip/SI, lower limbs
Undifferentiated (~10%)
Systemic JIA vs childhood lupus (ISAL Q&A)
Lupus: malar rash, renal disease (proteinuria, hematuria), neuropsychiatric features, anti-dsDNA and low complement. Systemic JIA: salmon rash with the fever, no dsDNA or low complement. Both can be ANA+ (sometimes Ro+).
  • Complications (children's joints are growing): flexion contracture, muscle wasting, leg-length discrepancy (overgrowth of the inflamed leg), TMJ disease (micrognathia and a retruded chin, reduced mouth opening, trouble eating, sleep apnea), growth impairment, uveitis. Uveitis risk: girls, young onset, oligoarticular, ANA+. In oligo and poly JIA the uveitis is silent (hence regular screening); in ERA, as in adult SpA, it is a red, painful eye.
  • NSAIDs: naproxen (available as a liquid), celecoxib in older children. Try them for about 4–6 weeks before escalating; general pediatricians should start them while the child waits (the Ontario target is to see JIA within 6 weeks of referral), and use them for flares on DMARDs/biologics. You don't need the biologic names for the exam.
  • Prognosis: only ~20–50% reach complete remission in adulthood; usually followed lifelong. Three courses: one flare then lifelong remission; remission with later flares; or chronic arthritis that never fully settles.
  • Vaccines: inactivated vaccines are always safe (injectable influenza only); avoid live vaccines (MMRV, nasal flu, yellow fever, BCG) on immunosuppression. Vaccinate before treatment; give MMRV ≥4 weeks before starting.
Fever + refusal to bear weight = septic until proven otherwise (Kocher: NWB, fever >38.5, WBC >12k, ESR >40; 3/4 = 93%). Post-viral afebrile hip limp = transient synovitis → NSAIDs. Night pain + bruising + weight loss + metaphyseal bands = leukemia. Night-time bilateral leg pain, otherwise well = growing pains → watch and wait. JIA: <16, ≥6 weeks; oligo = young girl, knee, ANA+, screen eyes; poly ≥5 joints; systemic = quotidian fever + rash → IL-1/IL-6.

guides.title: Week 39 · 9 MAPS: Upper Limb Imaging, POCUS & Cytopathology
guides.html:
MAPS · Anatomy

MAPS: Upper Limb Imaging, POCUS & Cytopathology

Week 39 · MSK III — OA, Spine & Pediatric Rheumatology
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The three multidisciplinary cases (cuff tear with CPPD, trans-scaphoid perilunate dislocation, gouty olecranon bursitis with ulnar neuropathy), plus POCUS and polarized-light microscopy.

Principles

  • Imaging of MSK injury always starts with plain X-rays to rule out fracture; add US, CT or MRI as the case requires.
  • For a suspected rotator cuff tear, MRI is the most sensitive and specific option (WFQ); ultrasound/POCUS is a quick bedside screen. (In the session, the resident thought X-ray + US was reasonable for this case and no further imaging was needed.)
  • Share clinical information with the radiologist and pathologist: requisitions matter.

Case 1: the tennis player's shoulder

55-year-old woman, chronic right shoulder pain, sudden severe pain while serving, then can't abduct.

  • X-ray: no fracture; amorphous density above the humeral head = calcific tendinopathy (supraspinatus). US: full-thickness supraspinatus tear with a complex (heterogeneous) effusion, i.e. abnormal fluid such as hemarthrosis or infection.
  • History checklist the resident taught: hand dominance, occupation and hobbies, substance use, anticoagulants (the effusion could be a bleed). Adhesive capsulitis loses both active and passive range, so check passive ROM for a mechanical block. Chronic supraspinatus insufficiency lets the humeral head ride up against the acromion: cuff tear arthropathy.
  • Posterior shoulder aspiration: find the tip of the acromion, go 2 fingerbreadths distal, then medial.
  • Supraspinatus initiates abduction (suprascapular nerve) and passes under the coracoacromial arch. The coracoacromial arch limits superior dislocation; superior GH support also comes from the coracohumeral and glenohumeral ligaments and the long head of biceps.
  • Differential: OA flare, gout, CPPD, septic arthritis, Milwaukee shoulder (rare), cuff tear/arthropathy, impingement, bursitis; less likely fracture, dislocation/labral injury, AC injury.
  • Requisition: age/sex, history, imaging findings, aspiration site, volume and colour; request Gram stain, culture, cell count, crystals.
  • Result: cloudy yellow fluid, WBC ~25,000 (neutrophils), Gram stain/culture negative, normal glucose, high protein; rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals = CPPD.

Synovial fluid analysis (cytopathology)

ComponentWhat it tells you
GrossVolume, colour, viscosity, clarity (clear, cloudy, bloody, purulent)
Cell count + differentialLow = non-inflammatory (OA); high with neutrophils = infection or crystal arthritis
SmearNormal background: macrophages, synovial lining cells
MicrobiologyGram stain, culture
ChemistryGlucose, protein, LDH (inflammation: high protein, normal glucose)
CrystalsPolarized light microscopy

Polarized light, step by step

  1. Brightfield first: find refractile structures.
  2. Add the analyzer (above the specimen) and polarizer (below), crossed: the background goes dark and birefringent crystals light up.
  3. Add the red compensator: colour relative to the compensator axis gives the sign.
Gout (MSU)Pseudogout (CPPD)
ShapeNeedleRhomboid/blocky
BirefringenceStrong negativeWeak positive
Parallel to compensatorYellowBlue
PerpendicularBlueYellow
CytologyOften intracellular in neutrophilsUsually extracellular
SettingMiddle-aged/older, first MTPElderly, knee/wrist/shoulder

Tophus histology = granulomatous inflammation: palisading histiocytes/giant cells around feathery amorphous crystal material (MSU often dissolves in processing). Tophi are removed for function, pain, cosmesis or infection.

Case 2: fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH) from a ladder

20-year-old, high-energy FOOSH, dorsal wrist deformity, tender over lunate/capitate, median nerve numbness, positive Tinel's at the carpal tunnel, delayed capillary refill in digit 1.

  • X-ray: dorsal dislocation of the carpus relative to the lunate + a fractured scaphoid = trans-scaphoid perilunate fracture-dislocation. In a lunate dislocation the lunate itself displaces volarly into the carpal tunnel.
  • Median nerve symptoms: the displaced carpus/lunate compresses the carpal tunnel contents.
  • Reading the wrist X-ray: on a PA the ulnar styloid sits on the outer edge of the ulna; trace the smooth carpal arcs (proximal row, then the proximal edge of the distal row): a step or gap means the carpus is disrupted. In the injury, the capitate sits dorsal to the lunate on the lateral view. Perilunate injury is high-energy (young manual workers), very commonly missed, and does very poorly without surgery.
  • Trauma history and exam: AMPLE with last meal (anaesthesia), head injury or neck pain (distracting injury), onset and progression of neuro symptoms, open wounds (prophylactic antibiotics), joint above and below, and two-point discrimination (5 vs 10 mm) in each nerve territory.
  • Median nerve motor test ("OK sign"): the patient makes a round "O" by flexing the thumb IP (FPL) and index DIP (FDP); a flat pinch with the finger pads doesn't test the median nerve.
  • Management: urgent closed reduction under sedation (likely highly unstable given the bony injury; wrist extension, traction in line with the deformity, then wrist flexion, keeping a thumb on the lunate), then reassess neurovascular status. If successful and the neuro deficit improves, the OR becomes less urgent. If it fails or is unstable: urgent open reduction, fixation (scaphoid headless compression screw, K-wires). A carpal tunnel release is done for anyone with a perilunate injury and median symptoms regardless (non-acutely if reduction succeeds). A scapholunate repair is probably unnecessary when the energy went through the scaphoid.
  • Don't-miss orthopaedic injuries: open injuries, dislocations, occult fractures (e.g. an undisplaced femoral neck fracture with a posterior hip dislocation), vascular injury, neurological compromise, compartment syndrome (tense compartments, pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch). Also: distal radius, Barton (shear distal radius fracture with carpal subluxation) and Galeazzi (distal radial shaft fracture with DRUJ injury) fractures.

Case 3: hot elbow with numb ring and little fingers

71-year-old with HTN, T2DM, obesity on hydrochlorothiazide: sudden red, warm, swollen elbow, firm nodules, numb and weak 4th/5th digits.

  • X-ray: posterior soft-tissue swelling with calcific densities and no joint effusion; US then MRI: a thick-walled enhancing olecranon bursitis with no extension into the elbow joint (so not septic arthritis). Aspirate: WBC ~40,000, needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent intracellular crystals = gout (tophi + thiazide).
  • Ulnar nerve is compressed as it passes behind the medial epicondyle through the cubital tunnel.
  • Ulnar nerve exam: Froment's sign (thumb IP flexes via FPL to substitute for a weak adductor pollicis), Wartenberg's sign (little finger drifts into abduction). High lesion: FCU + ulnar FDP + intrinsics weak; sensory loss palmar and dorsal 5th and ulnar half of 4th. Low (wrist) lesion: intrinsics only; dorsal sensation may be spared (dorsal branch leaves ~8 cm proximal to the pisiform).
  • Ulnar paradox: clawing is worse with a low lesion because FDP is still working.
  • A low lesion is at Guyon's canal (between the hook of hamate and the pisiform), e.g. mass effect from an ulnar artery thrombus.

Carpal tunnel anatomy (lab)

The carpal bones form an arch open anteriorly; the flexor retinaculum closes it into the tunnel, attaching to the hook of hamate and pisiform medially and the scaphoid and trapezium tubercles laterally (the lab figure labels the hook of hamate and trapezium). Elbow X-ray landmarks: olecranon, trochlea, capitulum, radial head, coronoid process.

POCUS

  • Elbow: posterior long- and short-axis views over the olecranon fossa (distal humerus, olecranon, posterior fat pad, epicondyles). Elbow flexed; long axis with the probe marker to the patient's head, short axis rotated 90° with the marker to the patient's right. An elevated posterior fat pad = elbow effusion or lipohemarthrosis (exit quiz: both). On X-ray, a raised anterior fat pad is the "sail sign", and any visible posterior fat pad sign also means an effusion.
  • Distal radius: three longitudinal views, radial, dorsal and volar, looking for cortical displacement or a buckle fracture.
Plain X-ray first. Can't abduct after a tennis serve = supraspinatus tear (MRI most sensitive). Aspirate: Gram/culture, count, crystals; high neutrophils = infection or crystal arthritis. Gout = needle, strong negative, yellow parallel, intracellular; CPPD = rhomboid, weak positive, blue parallel. Perilunate + scaphoid fracture → median nerve compromise → reduce, then OR + carpal tunnel release. Gouty olecranon bursitis → ulnar nerve at the cubital tunnel.

ISAL · Worksheet

Integrated Rheumatology Review (Weeks 38–39)

Week 39 · MSK III — OA, Spine & Pediatric Rheumatology
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The SLM05 comparison tables and the three ISAL cases: telling apart inflammatory arthritis, axial SpA, myositis, PMR and fibromyalgia; RA vs OA; and rheumatic disease in older adults.

The comparison worksheet (SLM05)

ConditionHistoryExamInvestigations
Inflammatory arthritisPain/stiffness worse with rest, better with activity (AM stiffness ≥30 min); swelling; ± constitutionalSwelling, joint-line tenderness, limited ROM, EAMs± high ESR/CRP, abnormal CBC; RF/anti-CCP; abnormal X-ray
Axial SpAInflammatory back/neck pain, ± hip; enthesitis, dactylitis, EAMs± limited spinal movement± ESR/CRP; HLA-B27; X-ray
Inflammatory myositisProximal weakness, ± rash, dyspneaProximal weakness, rash, ILD signsHigh CK, myositis antibodies, MRI, EMG
PMRPain + AM stiffness ≥30 min in ≥2 of shoulder girdle, neck, hip girdle; constitutionalLimited shoulder/neck/hip movement (pain), no weaknessHigh ESR/CRP, anemia, thrombocytosis; normal CK
FibromyalgiaWidespread pain + sleep/fatigue ≥3 months; mood, cognitive symptomsDiffuse tenderness onlyNormal

RA vs OA

RAOA
ExamSwelling, warmth, limited ROM, joint-line tenderness; boutonnière, swan neckLimited ROM, joint-line tenderness, crepitus; Heberden (DIP), Bouchard (PIP)
X-rayPeriarticular osteopenia, uniform narrowing, erosionsSubchondral sclerosis, cysts, osteophytes, non-uniform narrowing
JointsSymmetric MCP, PIP, wrist, MTP plus shoulders, elbows, knees, ankles; C-spineDIP, PIP, CMC1, first MTP, knees, hips, C- and L-spine

Seropositive vs seronegative: RA/lupus involve the C-spine only; SpA involves the SI joints ± the whole spine. Serology: RA = RF, anti-CCP; lupus = ANA, ENA, C3/C4; SpA = HLA-B27. Synovial fluid: non-inflammatory = clear, high viscosity, <2000 ×106/L; inflammatory = turbid, low viscosity, >2000; infection or crystals typically >50,000 with ~90% PMN, but only as a guideline: the MAPS CPPD aspirate was 25,000.

ISAL case 1: a hot knee in CKD

50-year-old with CKD, febrile, 5 days of a red, hot, swollen right knee. Next step: aspirate (cell count, crystals, culture) rather than blind antibiotics, colchicine or referral. Fluid: 65,000 WBC (80% PMN), culture negative, needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals; creatinine 200 → gout.

Best acute treatment here
Intra-articular glucocorticoid: NSAIDs are contraindicated (CKD), colchicine only works within 12–36 h (Dr. Yang said "~48 h" aloud; either way, not at day 5) and is poorly cleared in renal disease, and IA steroid is preferred over oral in a monoarthritis because it exposes the patient only to local side effects. With two joints you could inject both; with a polyarticular flare (five or more joints) use oral glucocorticoids (the exam won't ask you to choose between injecting 2 and 3). Acetaminophen won't treat inflammation.

Crystal colour check: CPPD is blue when parallel to the compensator (the ISAL audio says "perpendicular"; trust the table in the MAPS guide).

ISAL case 2: symmetric small-joint polyarthritis

32-year-old woman, 6 months of joint pain, 60 min AM stiffness, partial NSAID response, no back pain, symmetric small-joint synovitis → RA. First-line DMARD: methotrexate (not prednisone, which isn't disease-modifying; not a biologic first; not colchicine). Symptom relief: splint, ice, joint protection, NSAIDs, glucocorticoids.

ISAL case 3: an older woman who can't get dressed

66-year-old woman: 3 months of hip, then shoulder and neck pain and stiffness, 1 h in the morning, 10 lb weight loss, low energy, no weakness (just painful), normal exam otherwise. Hb 108, platelets 450, ESR 60, CRP 72; CK, calcium, PTH, TSH, SPEP normal → PMR.

  • Not RA: wrong joint pattern. Not myositis: no weakness, painful, normal CK. Not fibromyalgia: labs show inflammation.
  • Next: screen for GCA; low–medium dose glucocorticoid; refer to rheumatology.

Working up generalized pain

Basic bloodwork (CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, calcium, TSH, ± ESR/CRP, CK, SPEP) excludes most mimics of fibromyalgia: hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism/hypercalcemia, myeloma, infection, statin myopathy. Avoid ANA, RF and HLA-B27 at low pre-test probability (WFQ). Classic fibromyalgia: widespread tenderness, give-way weakness from pain, fatigue, headaches, IBS-like bowel symptoms, normal exam.

Rheumatic disease in older adults (CBL 39 objective)

ConditionClues
OA≥45, activity pain, <30 min stiffness, bony swelling, cool joints; X-ray LOSS
PMR>50, girdle stiffness, high ESR/CRP, dramatic steroid response, normal CK
GCA>50, headache, jaw claudication, vision; start high-dose steroids on suspicion, don't wait for the biopsy
Late-onset RA>60, often abrupt or PMR-like onset; RF/CCP, CRP
GoutDiuretics, CKD, alcohol; favours damaged (OA) joints; serum urate may be normal in a flare
CPPD"Elderly woman + swollen wrist = pseudogout"; knee/wrist; chondrocalcinosis

Safe prescribing in the elderly: prefer topical NSAIDs and scheduled acetaminophen; oral NSAIDs rarely safe (renal, CV, GI, anticoagulants, falls). Systemic glucocorticoid side effects depend on duration, so a short oral course is reasonable when many joints are involved.

Systemic glucocorticoid side effects (ISAL body map)

SystemEffects
EyeCataract, glaucoma, blurred vision
PsychiatricSleep and mood disturbance, psychosis
Cardiovascular / renalHypertension, raised lipoproteins; hypokalemia, edema
GIGastritis, peptic ulcer
EndocrineDiabetes/hyperglycemia, adrenal suppression
MSKOsteoporosis, avascular necrosis, myopathy
Fat / skinWeight gain, Cushingoid redistribution; striae, acne, hirsutism
ImmuneImmunosuppression, lymphocytopenia, neutrophilia

Scope notes from Dr. Yang: everything in the pre-week material, self-learning and lectures is fair game (including the antibody–disease pairs); drug names for biologics/tsDMARDs and the differences between drug families aren't expected; Sjögren's and MCTD aren't a focus. Dr. Rozenblyum: the MSK I shoulder lecture isn't on this exam; the hip and knee are examined in a rheumatology context (not hip fracture); she couldn't confirm either way about Ortho 1 (extremities).

Weakness + high CK = myositis; stiffness + high ESR/CRP + normal CK = PMR; widespread pain + normal labs = fibromyalgia. Hot knee: aspirate first; gout in CKD → IA steroid. RA first-line DMARD = methotrexate. RA X-ray = osteopenia + erosions; OA = sclerosis, cysts, osteophytes.
